citations.quote:
**(a) Data of a one-dimensional model.** A **one-dimensional model** is
declared by the following data: a fixed positive **mass** $m>0$, of dimension
$\mu$ read in kilograms ([[def-cm01-units]], [[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause
(v)); a **time window** $I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$, a nondegenerate open
interval read in seconds ([[def-interval]]); an open **configuration
domain** $Q\subseteq\mathbb R$, a nonempty open interval of the real line
read in metres; and a **force law**
$$F:I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad (t,x,v)\longmapsto F(t,x,v),$$
of dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$, read in newtons, subject to the **standing
regularity** of the framework: $F$ is continuous on $I_{0}\times Q\times
\mathbb R$ and locally Lipschitz in the state variable $(x,v)$ locally
uniformly in time ([[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]). The
framework's three-dimensional force branch is
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]]; the class declared here is a **restricted
model class** adopted at the same primitive level, in which the physical
position of a single label along one coordinate is the whole state. A model
whose force law fails the standing regularity is not a one-dimensional model
of this class. When a statement differentiates the force law or the potential,
the additional smoothness it needs is stated in that statement.

**(b) Motions.** Let $J\subseteq I_{0}$ be an interval with nonempty interior
(endpoints read with one-sided derivatives, as in
[[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]). A **motion** of
the model on $J$ is a curve $x:J\to Q$ of class $C^{2}$
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]) with
$$m\,x''(t)=F\bigl(t,x(t),x'(t)\bigr)\qquad(t\in J).$$
In the notation of the three-dimensional branch this is the scalar
restriction of its equation of motion clause (iv) to a single coordinate; the
motions of the present class are declared to be these curves. A **datum** at
time $t_{0}\in I_{0}$ is a triple $(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})$ with $x_{0}\in Q$ and
$v_{0}\in\mathbb R$; a motion $x$ **takes** the datum when $x(t_{0})=x_{0}$
and $x'(t_{0})=v_{0}$.

**(c) Phase system.** The **phase system** of the model is the first-order
system on the open set $I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R\subseteq\mathbb R^{3}$
with right-hand side
$$G_{F}(t,x,v):=\Bigl(v,\ \frac{F(t,x,v)}{m}\Bigr),$$
read as a system of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]];
its state variable is $z=(x,v)$. For an interval $J\subseteq I_0$ with
nonempty interior, a **phase solution** on $J$ means a differentiable curve
$z:J\to Q\times\mathbb R$ satisfying $z'(t)=G_F(t,z(t))$ for every $t\in J$,
with domain-relative derivatives at included endpoints. Equivalently, for
any $t_0\in J$ it is a solution in the cited IVP sense with datum
$(t_0,z(t_0))$. For a $C^2$ curve $x:J\to Q$, being a motion is equivalent
to $t\mapsto(x(t),x'(t))$ being a phase solution: the first component is
$x'=v$ and the second is $x''=F(t,x,x')/m$. Conversely a phase solution
$(x,v)$ has $x'=v$ and $v'=F(t,x,v)/m$; continuity of $F$ makes $v'$ continuous,
so $x$ is $C^2$ and is a motion. This is the argument of clause (c) of
[[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]] read in one
coordinate. Here $x$ is the **position** or **displacement** coordinate and
$v$ the **velocity** coordinate; both are read in the fixed inertial frame in
which the model is declared. The phase system inherits the standing
regularity: $G_{F}$ is continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable
locally uniformly in time, so the Picard–Lindelöf hypotheses of
[[thm-picard-lindelof-local-existence-and-uniqueness]] hold at every point of
its domain.

**(d) Potential presentation, residual forces and energy.** The model
**presents its force law through a potential** when it declares a function
$U:Q\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^{2}$ in the sense of clause (a) of
[[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]] of dimension
$\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$, read in joules, and a **residual force**
$d:I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ of the standing regularity of
(a), with
$$F(t,x,v)=-U'(x)+d(t,x,v)\qquad\bigl((t,x,v)\in I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R\bigr);$$
here $U'$ is the ordinary derivative. This is the one-coordinate case of the
potential presentation of [[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]] clause
(a) for a time- and velocity-independent potential, and the scalar
$U$ is a **potential energy** of the model's potential part. The model is a
**global potential model** (equivalently, in the framework's usage, a
**conservative model**) when $d\equiv0$; the term "conservative" is used only
in this sense, as recorded in that definition. For a conservative model the
**mechanical energy** is the function
$$E:Q\times\mathbb R\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad E(x,v):=\tfrac12 m v^{2}+U(x),$$
of dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$. For a model with declared residual
forces, the **mechanical energy along a motion** $x:J\to Q$ is
$E(t):=\tfrac12m\,x'(t)^{2}+U(x(t))$; it is defined along curve families even
though the force law is not presented through $U$ alone.

**(e) Equilibria.** A **time- and velocity-independent force law** on $Q$ is
one of the form $F(t,x,v)=f(x)$ for a function $f:Q\to\mathbb R$; the model
is then **autonomous**. For such a law, a point $x_{*}\in Q$ is an
**equilibrium** (or **rest position**) when $f(x_{*})=0$, and the phase-plane
point $(x_{*},0)$ is the corresponding **rest point** of the phase system;
the constant curve $x\equiv x_{*}$ is then a motion. When the force law is
presented as $f=-U'$ with $U$ of class $C^{2}$, the equilibria are exactly
the critical points of $U$:
$f(x_{*})=0\iff U'(x_{*})=0$. A point $x_{0}\in Q$ is a **strict local
minimum** of $U$ when $U(x)>U(x_{0})$ for every $x\in Q$ with $0<\lvert
x-x_{0}\rvert<r_{0}$ for some $r_{0}>0$. The **Lyapunov stability** and
**asymptotic stability** of a rest point of the autonomous phase system are
the notions of [[def-cm-equilibrium-and-lyapunov-stability]] applied to the
field $G_{F}$; they are not defined here anew.

**(f) Oscillator-type data.** Let $m>0$, $c\ge0$, $k\in\mathbb R$ and let
$f:I_{0}\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. A model **is of oscillator type with
data $(m,c,k,f)$** when its force law has the form
$$F(t,x,v)=f(t)-c\,v-k\,x\qquad\bigl((t,x,v)\in I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R\bigr)$$
with $Q$ a nonempty open interval containing $0$ when the equation is read
about the origin, and the parameters are read with dimensions $[c]=\mu\tau^{-1}$
(kilograms per second), $[k]=\mu\tau^{-2}$ (kilograms per second squared) and
$[f]=\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$ (newtons). For such a model the equation of motion is
the second-order equation $m\,x''+c\,x'+k\,x=f(t)$, and the motions are
exactly the restrictions of the solutions of the mathematical model of
[[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]] with the same data, by the
identification of that definition's phase system with the phase system (c).
The parameters $c$ and $k$ are model data: they enter the model's declaration
and are not derived by this item.

**(g) Status.** This item introduces vocabulary, objects, regularity and
dimensions; it contains no existence, uniqueness, conservation, stability or
boundedness assertion, no force law of nature and no measured value. In
particular, clause (a) **declares** the one-dimensional class rather than
deriving it from the three-dimensional branch, and clauses (d)-(f) only fix
which data a model of the class carries. Every later statement of this page
names the model data, the potential representative and the initial datum it
uses.

Let $F:M\to N$ be $C^1$, let $(U,\varphi)$ be a chart on $M$, let $(V,\psi)$ be
a chart on $N$ with $F(U)\subseteq V$, and let $K\subseteq U$ be compact. Then
every point of $K$ has an open neighbourhood $W\subseteq U$ with
$\overline W\subseteq U$ such that the coordinate representative
$\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}$ is Lipschitz on $\varphi(\overline W)$.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $F$ is **locally Lipschitz in the state variable, locally uniformly in time**, if every compact time-state cylinder $C\subseteq D$ has a finite $L\ge0$ such that

$$\|F(t,x)-F(t,y)\|_2\le L\|x-y\|_2$$

whenever $(t,x),(t,y)\in C$ have the same time coordinate.

On every compact time-state cylinder the state-variable inequality holds with one finite constant $L$. More generally, let $p\ge1$, let $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb R^p$, let $D_\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n\times\Lambda$ be open in its relative Euclidean topology, and let $F:D_\Lambda\to\mathbb R^n$. The parameter family is **locally Lipschitz in the state variable, locally uniform in time and parameters** when every compact time-state-parameter cylinder $C\subseteq D_\Lambda$ has one finite $L\ge0$ such that

$$\|F(t,x,\lambda)-F(t,y,\lambda)\|_2\le L\|x-y\|_2$$

whenever $(t,x,\lambda),(t,y,\lambda)\in C$ have the same time and parameter coordinates.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

Let $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ and $y:J\to\mathbb R^n$ solve the same IVP. The solution $y$ is an **extension** of $x$ when $I\subseteq J$ and $y|_I=x$. It is a proper extension when $I\subsetneq J$.

A solution is **maximal** when it has no proper extension. Its domain is its **maximal interval of existence**. A solution is **global** when its domain is the entire time projection allowed by the ODE domain; for a vector field on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$, this means domain $\mathbb R$.

Every initial value problem satisfying the Picard-Lindelof hypotheses has a unique maximal solution. Its domain is an open interval containing the initial time, and every other solution through the same data is its restriction.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$, and let $n\ge1$. The equation

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$$

is a **first-order system**. An **initial value problem** consists of this equation and data $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, written $x(t_0)=x_0$.

A **solution on an interval** $I$ is a function $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ such that $t_0\in I$, $(t,x(t))\in D$ for every $t\in I$, $x$ is differentiable on $I$ in the domain-relative sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], and

$$x(t_0)=x_0,\qquad x'(t)=F(t,x(t))\quad(t\in I).$$

Endpoints of $I$ use the corresponding one-sided, domain-relative derivative. A local solution is one whose interval contains a nondegenerate neighborhood of $t_0$ relative to the time projection of $D$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) and let
$f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]) and
differentiable at every point of $I$ that is interior to $I$
([[def-interior-closure-boundary-r]], [[def-derivative]]), with

$$f'(x) = 0 \qquad \text{at every interior point } x \text{ of } I .$$

Then $f$ is constant on $I$: there is a real $k$ with $f(x) = k$ for every
$x \in I$.

Consequently, if $f, g : I \to \mathbb{R}$ are both continuous on $I$ and both
differentiable at every interior point of $I$, with $f'(x) = g'(x)$ at every
interior point $x$, then there is a real $k$ with

$$f(x) \;=\; g(x) + k \qquad \text{for every } x \in I .$$

**Order-convexity of $I$ is essential and is not a convenience.** The
conclusion is false on a domain that falls into separate pieces, since a
function may be constant on each piece with different constants; nothing in the
proof would survive, because the mean value theorem is applied to the segment
joining two points of the domain and that segment must lie in the domain.

**The hypothesis is imposed only at interior points.** At an endpoint of $I$
nothing is asked at all: $f$ need not be differentiable there, and the proof
never evaluates a difference quotient at an endpoint, since it applies the mean
value theorem on a segment $[u,v] \subseteq I$ and uses the derivative only at
points of $(u,v)$, all of which are interior to $I$. What is *not* meant is that
the derivative at an endpoint is free to be nonzero: once $f$ is known to be
constant its difference quotient at an endpoint is constantly $0$, so wherever
$f'$ exists at an endpoint it is $0$ too. That is a consequence of the theorem,
not a hypothesis of it.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

derivations.claim: The phase field $G_{F}$ satisfies the hypotheses of [L3] on the open time-state domain $I_0\times Q\times\mathbb R$ by [L2]. Hence every initial state $(x_{0},v_{0})$ has exactly one maximal solution $z:J_{\max}\to Q\times\mathbb R$ of $z'=G_{F}(z)$ with $z(t_{0})=(x_{0},v_{0})$, with $J_{\max}$ open and containing $t_{0}$, and every solution of the phase system with the same initial state is a restriction of $z$; the maximal interval is contained in the time projection $I_0$ of this domain. By the biconditional of [L1] the first component $x$ of $z$ is a motion and the second is $x'$; and if $y$ is any motion with the same datum, then $t\mapsto(y(t),y'(t))$ is a solution of the phase system with the same initial state and hence a restriction of $z$, so $y$ is a restriction of $x$. This is clause 1.

Let $x:J\to Q$ be a motion and put $e(t):=E(x(t),x'(t))=\tfrac12 m\,x'(t)^{2}+U(x(t))$ for $t\in J$. At every interior point $t$ of $J$, $x'$ is differentiable with derivative $x''$ and $x$ is differentiable, so by [L4] the function $e$ is differentiable there with $$e'(t)=m\,x'(t)x''(t)+U'\bigl(x(t)\bigr)x'(t)=x'(t)\bigl(m\,x''(t)+U'(x(t))\bigr)=x'(t)\bigl(F(x(t))+U'(x(t))\bigr)=0,$$ where the equation of motion $m\,x''(t)=F(x(t))$ and $F=-U'$ were used. The curve $e$ is continuous on the interval $J$, so [L5] gives that $e$ is constant on $J$. This is clause 2.

Let $x:J\to Q$ be a motion with datum $(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})$ and $E_{0}=E(x_{0},v_{0})$. By step 1.2, $E(x(t),x'(t))=E_{0}$ for every $t\in J$; subtracting $U(x(t))$ gives $\tfrac12 m\,x'(t)^{2}=E_{0}-U(x(t))$. The left side is nonnegative, so $U(x(t))\le E_{0}$; and $x'(t)^{2}=2(E_{0}-U(x(t)))/m$. If $U(x(t))<E_{0}$ then the right side is strictly positive, and [L6] applied to $a=2(E_{0}-U(x(t)))/m>0$ gives $x'(t)=\pm\sqrt{a}$; while $x'(t)=0$ holds exactly when $U(x(t))=E_{0}$. Finally $(x(t),x'(t))\in\Sigma_{E_{0}}$ for every $t\in J$ because $E(x(t),x'(t))=E_{0}$, by the definition of the level set. This is clause 3.

Clause 4: by [L1], $x_{*}$ is an equilibrium exactly when $F(x_{*})=0$, that is $U'(x_{*})=0$. If so, the constant curve $x\equiv x_{*}$ has $x''\equiv0$ and $m\cdot0=F(x_{*})=0$, so it is a motion with datum $(t_{0},x_{*},0)$; by the uniqueness clause of step 1.1 it is the maximal motion with that datum. Conversely, if the maximal motion with datum $(t_{0},x_{*},0)$ is the constant curve $x\equiv x_{*}$, then substituting into the equation of motion gives $0=m\cdot0=F(x_{*})$, so $U'(x_{*})=0$. This is clause 4.

boundaries.reason: The statement quantifies over one model with a fixed nonempty open configuration interval and a single datum; no possibly empty family is quantified.

boundaries.evidence: Clause 3 gives the two distinct square-root values for U(x)<E0; at U(x)=E0 the energy identity gives exactly x′=0. Both directions of this zero-velocity equivalence are checked in Proof 2.1.
The model is one-dimensional with one label by its declaration; the formula and conservation at steps 1.2 and 2.1 are uniform in the single coordinate.
A datum with v_0=0 and x_0 an equilibrium is the constant motion of step 3.1; no division by m or by a vanishing quantity occurs (m>0 is fixed).

Motions are defined on intervals with nonempty interior; step 1.2 concludes constancy of the energy using the zero derivative at interior points and continuity on the interval, as the supplier requires.

boundaries.reason: The argument applies a maximal-solution theorem and differentiates an explicit composition; no selection from a family is made.

boundaries.evidence: Clause 4 from equilibrium U'(x_*)=0 to the constant maximal motion is step 3.1.
Clause 4 from the constant maximal motion back to U'(x_*)=0 is step 3.1, by substitution into the equation of motion.

risk_review.notes: Checked all four steps: continuous locally state-Lipschitz field on open I0 × Q × R; unique maximal C2 motion; energy derivative vanishes and continuity covers included endpoints; m>0 gives speed formula and both zero-speed directions; rest motion is constant on I0. No global boundedness or empirical conclusion. Exact ODE, derivative and square-root suppliers match hypotheses.

citations.quote:
Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $M:\Omega\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ be of class $C^2$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) with $M(q)$ symmetric and positive definite for every $q\in\Omega$, that is $v^{\mathsf T}M(q)v>0$ for every nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $U:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$. The matrix field $M$ is the **kinetic metric field** and $U$ the **potential** of the data in the chart $\Omega$.

Coordinates and matrix entries are indexed by $0\le i,j,k<n$, as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. Vectors are read as columns: for $A\in M_n(\mathbb R)$, $(Av)_i:=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}A_{ij}v_j$, and $v^{\mathsf T}Av:=\sum_{i,j=0}^{n-1}v_iA_{ij}v_j$.

Define, for $(q,v)\in\Omega\times\mathbb R^n$, the **kinetic energy**, **Lagrangian** and **energy**

$$T(q,v):=\tfrac12v^{\mathsf T}M(q)v,\qquad L(q,v):=T(q,v)-U(q),\qquad E(q,v):=T(q,v)+U(q),$$

and, for $q\in\Omega$ and $v\in\mathbb R^n$, the matrix

$$D_qM(q)[v]:=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}v_k\,\partial_kM(q),\qquad\bigl(\partial_kM(q)\bigr)_{ij}=\partial_kM_{ij}(q)\quad(0\le i,j,k<n).$$

The **mechanical vector field** of the data is the map

$$G:\Omega\times\mathbb R^n\longrightarrow\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n,\qquad G(q,v)=\Bigl(v,\ M(q)^{-1}\bigl(\tfrac12\nabla_q(v^{\mathsf T}M(q)v)-\bigl(D_qM(q)[v]\bigr)v-\nabla U(q)\bigr)\Bigr),$$

where $\nabla_q$ and $\nabla U$ are Euclidean gradients ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]) and $M(q)^{-1}$ is the inverse of the positive definite matrix $M(q)$ ([[def-invertible-matrix-and-general-linear-group]], [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). The **mechanical system** in the chart is the first-order system

$$q'(t)=v(t),\qquad v'(t)=M(q(t))^{-1}\Bigl(\tfrac12\nabla_qf\bigl(q(t),v(t)\bigr)-\bigl(D_qM(q(t))[v(t)]\bigr)v(t)-\nabla U(q(t))\Bigr),\qquad f(q,v):=v^{\mathsf T}M(q)v .$$

A point $q_* \in\Omega$ is a **mechanical equilibrium** when $\nabla U(q_*)=0$.

Adopt a one-dimensional model $(m,I_{0},Q,F)$ of
[[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]], with phase system
$G_{F}(t,x,v)=(v,F(t,x,v)/m)$.

**(a) Phase plane and phase curves.** The **phase plane** of the model is
$\mathbb R^{2}$ with coordinates $(x,v)$, where $x$ is the position and $v$
the velocity coordinate of clause (b) of [[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]].
They are real numerical SI coordinates: if $X_{\rm phys}$ and $V_{\rm phys}$
are the corresponding physical position and velocity, then
$x=X_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm m)$ and
$v=V_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm{m/s})$ ([[def-cm01-units]]). The **phase domain**
of the model is the open set $I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R$ of (time,
position, velocity) triples. The phase plane is read with the Euclidean
structure and norm $\lVert(x,v)\rVert_{2}=\sqrt{x^{2}+v^{2}}$ on these
dimensionless numerical coordinates ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]);
physical displacement and velocity are not added as dimensionful quantities.
Distances used below are those of this norm. For a curve family
$x:J\to Q$ of class $C^{1}$ its **phase curve** is
$t\mapsto(x(t),x'(t))$; when $x$ is a motion of the model the phase curve is
the corresponding solution of the phase system.

**(b) The energy function of a conservative model.** Let the model be a
global potential model of clause (d) of
[[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]] with potential $U$ of
class $C^{2}$, so that $F=-U'$. The **energy function** of the model is
$$E:Q\times\mathbb R\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad E(x,v):=\tfrac12 m v^{2}+U(x),$$
of dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (joules). For $E_{0}\in\mathbb R$ the
**energy level set** of $E_{0}$ and the **energy sublevel set** of $E_{0}$
are
$$\Sigma_{E_{0}}:=\{(x,v)\in Q\times\mathbb R:E(x,v)=E_{0}\},\qquad S_{E_{0}}:=\{(x,v)\in Q\times\mathbb R:E(x,v)\le E_{0}\}.$$

**(c) Turning positions and turning points.** Let the model be as in (b).
A point $x\in Q$ is a **turning position** of the energy $E_{0}$ when
$U(x)=E_{0}$, and the phase-plane point $(x,0)$ is the corresponding
**turning point** of $E_{0}$. A turning position at which $U'$ does not
vanish is a **simple turning position**. In the one-coordinate reading of
[[def-cm-mechanical-vector-field-and-energy-in-a-chart]] the potential
difference $U(x)-E_{0}$ is the sign-controlling quantity for the velocity of
a motion of energy $E_{0}$; the statements of that kind are the content of
the conservation theorem of this page and are not made here.

**(d) Rest points and stability vocabulary.** For a model with a time- and
velocity-independent force law $f$, the equilibria, rest points, strict local
minima and the Lyapunov and asymptotic stability of a rest point are those of
clause (e) of [[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]], read for
the phase system $G_{F}$; Lyapunov stability is the notion of
[[def-cm-equilibrium-and-lyapunov-stability]] and linear stability is that of
[[def-cm-orbital-and-linear-stability]], applied to $G_{F}$ at its rest
point. For an oscillator-type model with data $(m,c,k,f)$ of clause (f) of
[[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]] the phase system is the
phase-plane system of [[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]], and the
phase-plane reading of its equilibria is the one recorded there.

**(e) Status.** This item fixes geometric objects and reads mathematical
stability vocabulary for the scalar phase system; it asserts no conservation
of energy, no containment of a phase curve in a level set, no boundedness of
level sets and no measured value.

Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $M:\Omega\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ be a $C^2$ field of symmetric positive definite matrices, let $U:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$, let $q_0\in\Omega$ with $\nabla U(q_0)=0$, and suppose $q_0$ is a **strict local minimum** of $U$: there is $r_0>0$ with $\overline B(q_0,r_0)\subseteq\Omega$ and

$$U(q)>U(q_0)\qquad(0<\|q-q_0\|_2<r_0).$$

Let $G$ be the mechanical vector field of [[def-cm-mechanical-vector-field-and-energy-in-a-chart]] on $\Omega\times\mathbb R^n$, with energy $E(q,v)=\tfrac12v^{\mathsf T}M(q)v+U(q)$. Then $(q_0,0)$ is a Lyapunov stable equilibrium of $(q',v')=G(q,v)$ in the sense of [[def-cm-equilibrium-and-lyapunov-stability]]: for every $\varepsilon>0$ with $\overline B((q_0,0),\varepsilon)\subseteq\Omega\times\mathbb R^n$ there is $\delta>0$ such that every maximal solution $(q,v)$ with $\|(q(0),v(0))-(q_0,0)\|_2<\delta$ is defined for all $t\ge0$ and satisfies

$$\|(q(t),v(t))-(q_0,0)\|_2<\varepsilon\qquad(t\ge0).$$

No asymptotic stability is asserted.

Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $M:\Omega\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ be a $C^2$ field of symmetric positive definite matrices, let $U:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$, and let $q_0\in\Omega$ be a mechanical equilibrium, that is $\nabla U(q_0)=0$ ([[def-cm-mechanical-vector-field-and-energy-in-a-chart]]). Let $G$ be the mechanical vector field on $\Omega\times\mathbb R^n$. Then:

1. $G$ is totally differentiable at $(q_0,0)$ ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]]) and, writing $D^2U(q_0)$ for the Hessian matrix ([[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]]),

$$DG(q_0,0)(\delta q,\delta v)=\Bigl(\delta v,\ -M(q_0)^{-1}D^2U(q_0)\,\delta q\Bigr)\qquad(\delta q,\delta v\in\mathbb R^n);$$

2. consequently the linearised equation at the equilibrium is

$$\xi''=-M(q_0)^{-1}D^2U(q_0)\,\xi,\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad M(q_0)\xi''+D^2U(q_0)\,\xi=0,$$

a constant-coefficient system whose mass matrix $M(q_0)$ is symmetric positive definite and whose stiffness matrix $D^2U(q_0)$ is symmetric ([[cor-hessian-is-symmetric]]);
3. if in addition $q_0$ is a strict local minimum of $U$, then $K:=D^2U(q_0)$ is non-negative, so the hypotheses of [[thm-cm-quadratic-mode-decomposition]] are satisfied by $M(q_0)$ and $K$, and the linearised system is exactly the constant-coefficient quadratic system of that theorem with mass matrix $M(q_0)$ and stiffness $K$; its modes are the normal modes of the linearisation.

**(a) Data of a one-dimensional model.** A **one-dimensional model** is
declared by the following data: a fixed positive **mass** $m>0$, of dimension
$\mu$ read in kilograms ([[def-cm01-units]], [[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause
(v)); a **time window** $I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$, a nondegenerate open
interval read in seconds ([[def-interval]]); an open **configuration
domain** $Q\subseteq\mathbb R$, a nonempty open interval of the real line
read in metres; and a **force law**
$$F:I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad (t,x,v)\longmapsto F(t,x,v),$$
of dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$, read in newtons, subject to the **standing
regularity** of the framework: $F$ is continuous on $I_{0}\times Q\times
\mathbb R$ and locally Lipschitz in the state variable $(x,v)$ locally
uniformly in time ([[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]). The
framework's three-dimensional force branch is
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]]; the class declared here is a **restricted
model class** adopted at the same primitive level, in which the physical
position of a single label along one coordinate is the whole state. A model
whose force law fails the standing regularity is not a one-dimensional model
of this class. When a statement differentiates the force law or the potential,
the additional smoothness it needs is stated in that statement.

**(b) Motions.** Let $J\subseteq I_{0}$ be an interval with nonempty interior
(endpoints read with one-sided derivatives, as in
[[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]). A **motion** of
the model on $J$ is a curve $x:J\to Q$ of class $C^{2}$
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]) with
$$m\,x''(t)=F\bigl(t,x(t),x'(t)\bigr)\qquad(t\in J).$$
In the notation of the three-dimensional branch this is the scalar
restriction of its equation of motion clause (iv) to a single coordinate; the
motions of the present class are declared to be these curves. A **datum** at
time $t_{0}\in I_{0}$ is a triple $(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})$ with $x_{0}\in Q$ and
$v_{0}\in\mathbb R$; a motion $x$ **takes** the datum when $x(t_{0})=x_{0}$
and $x'(t_{0})=v_{0}$.

**(c) Phase system.** The **phase system** of the model is the first-order
system on the open set $I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R\subseteq\mathbb R^{3}$
with right-hand side
$$G_{F}(t,x,v):=\Bigl(v,\ \frac{F(t,x,v)}{m}\Bigr),$$
read as a system of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]];
its state variable is $z=(x,v)$. For an interval $J\subseteq I_0$ with
nonempty interior, a **phase solution** on $J$ means a differentiable curve
$z:J\to Q\times\mathbb R$ satisfying $z'(t)=G_F(t,z(t))$ for every $t\in J$,
with domain-relative derivatives at included endpoints. Equivalently, for
any $t_0\in J$ it is a solution in the cited IVP sense with datum
$(t_0,z(t_0))$. For a $C^2$ curve $x:J\to Q$, being a motion is equivalent
to $t\mapsto(x(t),x'(t))$ being a phase solution: the first component is
$x'=v$ and the second is $x''=F(t,x,x')/m$. Conversely a phase solution
$(x,v)$ has $x'=v$ and $v'=F(t,x,v)/m$; continuity of $F$ makes $v'$ continuous,
so $x$ is $C^2$ and is a motion. This is the argument of clause (c) of
[[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]] read in one
coordinate. Here $x$ is the **position** or **displacement** coordinate and
$v$ the **velocity** coordinate; both are read in the fixed inertial frame in
which the model is declared. The phase system inherits the standing
regularity: $G_{F}$ is continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable
locally uniformly in time, so the Picard–Lindelöf hypotheses of
[[thm-picard-lindelof-local-existence-and-uniqueness]] hold at every point of
its domain.

**(d) Potential presentation, residual forces and energy.** The model
**presents its force law through a potential** when it declares a function
$U:Q\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^{2}$ in the sense of clause (a) of
[[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]] of dimension
$\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$, read in joules, and a **residual force**
$d:I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ of the standing regularity of
(a), with
$$F(t,x,v)=-U'(x)+d(t,x,v)\qquad\bigl((t,x,v)\in I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R\bigr);$$
here $U'$ is the ordinary derivative. This is the one-coordinate case of the
potential presentation of [[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]] clause
(a) for a time- and velocity-independent potential, and the scalar
$U$ is a **potential energy** of the model's potential part. The model is a
**global potential model** (equivalently, in the framework's usage, a
**conservative model**) when $d\equiv0$; the term "conservative" is used only
in this sense, as recorded in that definition. For a conservative model the
**mechanical energy** is the function
$$E:Q\times\mathbb R\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad E(x,v):=\tfrac12 m v^{2}+U(x),$$
of dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$. For a model with declared residual
forces, the **mechanical energy along a motion** $x:J\to Q$ is
$E(t):=\tfrac12m\,x'(t)^{2}+U(x(t))$; it is defined along curve families even
though the force law is not presented through $U$ alone.

**(e) Equilibria.** A **time- and velocity-independent force law** on $Q$ is
one of the form $F(t,x,v)=f(x)$ for a function $f:Q\to\mathbb R$; the model
is then **autonomous**. For such a law, a point $x_{*}\in Q$ is an
**equilibrium** (or **rest position**) when $f(x_{*})=0$, and the phase-plane
point $(x_{*},0)$ is the corresponding **rest point** of the phase system;
the constant curve $x\equiv x_{*}$ is then a motion. When the force law is
presented as $f=-U'$ with $U$ of class $C^{2}$, the equilibria are exactly
the critical points of $U$:
$f(x_{*})=0\iff U'(x_{*})=0$. A point $x_{0}\in Q$ is a **strict local
minimum** of $U$ when $U(x)>U(x_{0})$ for every $x\in Q$ with $0<\lvert
x-x_{0}\rvert<r_{0}$ for some $r_{0}>0$. The **Lyapunov stability** and
**asymptotic stability** of a rest point of the autonomous phase system are
the notions of [[def-cm-equilibrium-and-lyapunov-stability]] applied to the
field $G_{F}$; they are not defined here anew.

**(f) Oscillator-type data.** Let $m>0$, $c\ge0$, $k\in\mathbb R$ and let
$f:I_{0}\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. A model **is of oscillator type with
data $(m,c,k,f)$** when its force law has the form
$$F(t,x,v)=f(t)-c\,v-k\,x\qquad\bigl((t,x,v)\in I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R\bigr)$$
with $Q$ a nonempty open interval containing $0$ when the equation is read
about the origin, and the parameters are read with dimensions $[c]=\mu\tau^{-1}$
(kilograms per second), $[k]=\mu\tau^{-2}$ (kilograms per second squared) and
$[f]=\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$ (newtons). For such a model the equation of motion is
the second-order equation $m\,x''+c\,x'+k\,x=f(t)$, and the motions are
exactly the restrictions of the solutions of the mathematical model of
[[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]] with the same data, by the
identification of that definition's phase system with the phase system (c).
The parameters $c$ and $k$ are model data: they enter the model's declaration
and are not derived by this item.

**(g) Status.** This item introduces vocabulary, objects, regularity and
dimensions; it contains no existence, uniqueness, conservation, stability or
boundedness assertion, no force law of nature and no measured value. In
particular, clause (a) **declares** the one-dimensional class rather than
deriving it from the three-dimensional branch, and clauses (d)-(f) only fix
which data a model of the class carries. Every later statement of this page
names the model data, the potential representative and the initial datum it
uses.

Let $m>0$, $c\ge0$ and $k\in\mathbb R$ be given real numbers, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $f:I\to\mathbb R$ be continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). The **damped driven oscillator model** with data $(m,c,k,f)$ is the second-order equation

$$m\,x''(t)+c\,x'(t)+k\,x(t)=f(t),\qquad t\in I .$$

A **solution** of the model on an interval $J\subseteq I$ with nonempty interior is a twice differentiable $x:J\to\mathbb R$ such that the identity holds for every $t\in J$, derivatives being ordinary real derivatives ([[def-derivative]], [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). The model is called **homogeneous** when $f\equiv 0$, **undamped** when $c=0$, and **strictly damped** when $c>0$.

The **phase-plane equation** of the model has right-hand side

$$G_f:I\times\mathbb R^2\longrightarrow\mathbb R^2,\qquad G_f(t,x,v):=\Bigl(v,\ \frac{f(t)-c\,v-k\,x}{m}\Bigr).$$

Here $\mathbb R^2$ is the **phase plane**, with coordinates $(x,v)$, where $x$ is the **displacement** and $v$ the **velocity**. For an interval $J\subseteq I$ with nonempty interior, a differentiable curve $z=(x,v):J\to\mathbb R^2$ solves the phase-plane equation when $z'(t)=G_f(t,z(t))$ for every $t\in J$, using the domain-relative derivative at any included endpoint ([[def-derivative]]). If $x$ is a solution of the model on $J$, then $t\mapsto(x(t),x'(t))$ solves this equation; conversely, if $t\mapsto(x(t),v(t))$ solves it, then $v=x'$ and $x$ is a solution of the model on $J$. When $J$ is open, this is the first-order system of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]] on the open domain $J\times\mathbb R^2$. For the homogeneous model the right-hand side is written $G_0(x,v)=(v,-(cv+kx)/m)$.

The **characteristic polynomial** of the model is

$$p(\lambda):=m\lambda^2+c\lambda+k,$$

with **discriminant** $\Delta:=c^2-4mk$. When $k>0$ define the **undamped frequency** $\omega_0:=\sqrt{k/m}$, the **damping rate** $\gamma:=c/(2m)$ and, when $4mk>c^2$, the **damped frequency** $\omega:=\sqrt{k/m-\gamma^2}=\sqrt{4mk-c^2}/(2m)$; the corresponding square roots are the nonnegative real ones.

**(i) Setting.** Work in the one-dimensional model class of
[[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]] with time window
$I_{0}=\mathbb R$, configuration domain $Q=\mathbb R$, a fixed mass $m>0$
and a **spring constant** $k>0$ of dimension $\mu\tau^{-2}$, read in newtons
per metre ([[def-cm01-units]]). The **harmonic model** is the model whose
force law is the **linear restoring force**
$$F(x,v):=-k\,x .$$
Its equation of motion is $m\,x''=-k\,x$, equivalently $m\,x''+k\,x=0$; the
model is autonomous and velocity-independent, and its potential is
$$U(x):=\tfrac12 k\,x^{2},$$
of dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (joules), which presents the force law in
the sense of clause (d) of [[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]]:
$U$ is of class $C^{2}$ in that clause's sense, and
$-U'(x)=-k\,x=F(x)$ ([[lem-derivative-of-a-power]],
[[def-derivative]]). The harmonic model is therefore a **conservative**
model of the class, with the potential representative $U$ declared above and
no residual force.

**(ii) Regularity and framework status.** Let
$X:=x_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm m)$ and
$V:=v_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm{m/s})$ be the dimensionless numerical SI state
coordinates (the real state coordinates in the displayed force-map signature),
and let $K:=k_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm{N/m})$ be the numerical
spring constant. In this representation the numerical force map
$\widehat F:=F_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm N)$ is
$\widehat F(X,V)=-KX$, so
$\lvert\widehat F(X,V)-\widehat F(X',V')\rvert\le
K\,\lVert(X,V)-(X',V')\rVert_{2}$. It is therefore locally Lipschitz in the
state variable with global numerical-coordinate constant $K$, uniformly in
time ([[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]). The harmonic model is
thus an admissible model of the class of clause (a) of
[[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]], and the existence,
uniqueness and conservation statements of this page apply to it. It is
adopted as a restricted model class of the framework, at the same primitive
level as the force maps of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]]: the force law
is model input.

**(iii) Physical reading and regime.** The model idealizes a **restoring
force linear in the displacement**: an ideal spring, or the quadratic
approximation of a potential $U$ near a strict local minimum $x_{*}$ with $U''(x_*)>0$, where
the Taylor expansion of the effective potential begins with the quadratic
term $\tfrac12 U''(x_{*})(x-x_{*})^{2}$ and the linearized equation carries
the **effective spring constant** $U''(x_{*})$ (the sources' linearization
procedure). The model is adopted for a stated regime — displacements so
small that the neglected remainder of the potential is adequate for the
purpose at hand — and it is **not** claimed to describe large-amplitude
oscillations, nonlinear springs, plasticity, or any given real system. The
coefficient $k$ is a model parameter, not a constant of the framework; when
its value is taken from a calibration experiment, that value is an empirical
premise carrying the apparatus conditions and the measurement uncertainty,
and the framework asserts none of it here. The linear form is the simplest
restoring law satisfying the standing regularity; that is a modelling
convenience, not a derivation.

**(iv) Status.** Adopted assumption of the framework when a model invokes
it; it selects no law of nature on its own. Every consequence below is a
conditional statement about the declared equation of motion.

Let $F:M\to N$ be $C^1$, let $(U,\varphi)$ be a chart on $M$, let $(V,\psi)$ be
a chart on $N$ with $F(U)\subseteq V$, and let $K\subseteq U$ be compact. Then
every point of $K$ has an open neighbourhood $W\subseteq U$ with
$\overline W\subseteq U$ such that the coordinate representative
$\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}$ is Lipschitz on $\varphi(\overline W)$.

Every initial value problem satisfying the Picard-Lindelof hypotheses has a unique maximal solution. Its domain is an open interval containing the initial time, and every other solution through the same data is its restriction.

derivations.claim: By [L1] the phase field $G_{F}$ of the model is the mechanical vector field of the mathematical data $(n,\Omega,M,U)=(1,Q,m,U)$ with the constant positive definite metric field $M\equiv m$. On intervals $J\subseteq I_0$, the phase curves of model motions are exactly the solutions $(q,v)$ of that mechanical system; unrestricted solutions are model motions only on their restrictions to the declared time window. Its energy is $E$. At the strict minimum, the difference quotient $(U(x_*+h)-U(x_*))/h$ is nonnegative for small $h>0$ and nonpositive for small $h<0$. Its common two-sided limit $U'(x_*)$ is therefore zero, as required by [L2] and [L3].

Clause 1. Let $\varepsilon>0$ with $\overline B((x_{*},0),\varepsilon)\subseteq Q\times\mathbb R$. Apply [L2] with $\Omega=Q$, $M\equiv m$, the potential $U$ and $q_{0}=x_{*}$: it produces $\delta>0$ such that every maximal solution $(q,v)$ of the mechanical system with $\lVert(q(0),v(0))-(x_{*},0)\rVert_{2}<\delta$ is defined for all $t\ge0$ and satisfies $\lVert(q(t),v(t))-(x_{*},0)\rVert_{2}<\varepsilon$ for all $t\ge0$. Now let $x:J\to Q$ be a motion of the model and $t_{0}\in J$ with $\lVert(x(t_{0}),x'(t_{0}))-(x_{*},0)\rVert_{2}<\delta$. The phase system is autonomous, so the translate $s\mapsto(x(t_{0}+s),x'(t_{0}+s))$, defined for $s$ with $t_{0}+s\in J$, is a solution of the same system with initial value $(x(t_{0}),x'(t_{0}))$ at $s=0$; it has a unique maximal extension for this unrestricted autonomous equation by [L5], and by step 1.1 and the defining property of $\delta$ that extension is defined for all $s\ge0$ and stays at distance $<\varepsilon$ from $(x_{*},0)$. Translating the maximal extension back yields a maximal curve whose domain contains $[t_{0},\infty)$ and which agrees with $x$ on $J$, and $\lVert(x(t)-x_{*},x'(t))\rVert_{2}<\varepsilon$ for all $t\ge t_{0}$. Since $\varepsilon$ was arbitrary, $(x_{*},0)$ is Lyapunov stable in the sense of [[def-cm-equilibrium-and-lyapunov-stability]].

Clause 2, differentiability and linearised equation. $U$ is $C^{2}$, so $D^{2}U(x_{*})=U''(x_{*})$ exists and $x_{*}$ is a mechanical equilibrium because $U'(x_{*})=0$ at a strict local minimum. Applying [L3] with $q_{0}=x_{*}$, $M(q_{0})=m$ and $D^{2}U(q_{0})=U''(x_{*})$ gives the displayed total derivative and the linearised equation $m\xi''+U''(x_{*})\xi=0$. By [L4] this is exactly the oscillator-type model with data $(m,0,U''(x_{*}),0)$. If $U''(x_{*})>0$, then $k:=U''(x_{*})>0$ and [L4] identifies the equation with that of the harmonic model with spring constant $k$; the frequency $\sqrt{k/m}$ is the undamped frequency $\omega_{0}$ attached to the data $(m,0,k,0)$ by [[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]], and it is quoted here only as the linearised frequency, not as a property of the nonlinear motion.

boundaries.reason: The strict local minimum and the ball of the stability quantifier are nonempty by hypothesis; no empty family is quantified.

boundaries.evidence: The zero displacement case is the equilibrium itself: U'(x_*)=0 and (x_*,0) is the fixed point whose stability is asserted, applied at step 2.1.
The instance n=1 of the mechanical system is identified at step 1.1; the energy-stability theorem is applied in that dimension.

boundaries.reason: The statement explicitly assumes a strict local minimum; weak minima and vanishing U''(x_*) are excluded from the hypotheses, as recorded in the statement and remarks.
No interval endpoint or boundary of the time domain enters; stability is a statement about the half-line t>=t_0 and the ball radius is an arbitrary admissible one.
The argument applies a fixed theorem and checks its hypotheses; no selection is made.
The item asserts stability and a linearisation identity; it is not stated as an equivalence.

The Statement uses a strict local potential minimum as a sufficient condition for Lyapunov stability and computes the linearization; it does not assert that every stable rest point must be a strict minimum.

All-time bounds use unrestricted autonomous extension rather than enlarging I0; linearization frequency requires U second derivative positive. No attraction or empirical assertion.
