citations.quote:
**(i) Setting.** Work in the one-dimensional model class of
[[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]] with time window
$I_{0}=\mathbb R$, configuration domain $Q=\mathbb R$, a fixed mass $m>0$,
the spring constant $k>0$ of [[post-cm04-harmonic-model]], and a **drag
coefficient** $c\ge0$ of dimension $\mu\tau^{-1}$, read in kilograms per
second ([[def-cm01-units]]). The model's force law is declared through the
additive composition of force contributions, in the sense of clause (v) of
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]], read in one coordinate:
$$F(x,v)=-k\,x-c\,v .$$

The **damped oscillator model** is the one-dimensional model with this force
law; its equation of motion is
$$m\,x''+c\,x'+k\,x=0,$$
and its data $(m,c,k,0)$ are oscillator-type data in the sense of clause (f)
of [[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]]. The model is
autonomous and depends on the velocity; it is **undamped** when $c=0$, in
which case it is exactly the harmonic model of [[post-cm04-harmonic-model]],
and **strictly damped** when $c>0$.

**(ii) Potential presentation with a residual force.** The model presents its
force law through the harmonic potential $U(x)=\tfrac12kx^{2}$ of
[[post-cm04-harmonic-model]] together with the **residual force**
$$d(t,x,v)=-c\,v,$$
in the sense of clause (d) of [[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]]:
$F(x,v)=-U'(x)+d(t,x,v)$. The mechanical energy of the model is therefore
the function $E(x,v)=\tfrac12mv^{2}+\tfrac12kx^{2}$ of clause (d), defined
along every motion; the drag force is not presented through a potential and
the model is not a global potential model when $c>0$.

**(iii) Regularity.** Let
$X:=x_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm m)$ and
$V:=v_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm{m/s})$ be the dimensionless numerical SI state
coordinates (the real state coordinates in the displayed force-map signature),
and let $K:=k_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm{N/m})$,
$C:=c_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm{kg/s})$ be the numerical coefficients. The
numerical force map $\widehat F:=F_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm N)$ is
$\widehat F(X,V)=-KX-CV$, so
$$\lvert\widehat F(X,V)-\widehat F(X',V')\rvert\le K\lvert X-X'\rvert+C\lvert V-V'\rvert\le(K+C)\,\lVert(X,V)-(X',V')\rVert_{2}.$$
The real number $K+C$ is a Lipschitz constant for this normalized numerical
coordinate map; the dimensionful coefficients $k$ and $c$ are not added.
The force map is continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable,
uniformly in time ([[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]). It is an
admissible force law of the class of clause (a) of
[[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]], and its equation is
exactly the homogeneous model $m\,x''+cx'+kx=0$ of
[[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]].

**(iv) Physical status and regime.** The drag term is a **phenomenological**
constitutive model, adopted rather than derived: it represents the net force
of a medium whose microscopic state is not part of the model. The linear
velocity-proportional form is a restricted regime — slow motion through a
viscous medium, of which the Stokes force $c=6\pi\eta a$ is the recorded
example in the framework's drag postulate [[post-cm02-drag]] — and the
coefficient $c$ is a model parameter depending on body and medium. Other
regimes are different models: drag growing quadratically with speed, or
Coulomb sliding friction, whose force contains the factor $v/\lvert v\rvert$
and is undefined at $v=0$ and is not of the standing regularity. The model
also neglects the random component of the environment's force; the recorded
source states that this neglect is admissible only in a stated energy regime,
in which the oscillator's energy greatly exceeds the energy scale of the
environment's fluctuations. No value of $c$, $m$ or $k$ is asserted, and a
measured value used in an application is an empirical premise with its own
conditions and uncertainty.

**(v) Status.** Adopted assumption of the framework when a model invokes it;
the damped oscillator selects no law of nature on its own, and no
fluctuation–dissipation relation is asserted. Its conditional consequences
are the subject of the damped-motion theorems of this page.

**(a) Data of a one-dimensional model.** A **one-dimensional model** is
declared by the following data: a fixed positive **mass** $m>0$, of dimension
$\mu$ read in kilograms ([[def-cm01-units]], [[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause
(v)); a **time window** $I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$, a nondegenerate open
interval read in seconds ([[def-interval]]); an open **configuration
domain** $Q\subseteq\mathbb R$, a nonempty open interval of the real line
read in metres; and a **force law**
$$F:I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad (t,x,v)\longmapsto F(t,x,v),$$
of dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$, read in newtons, subject to the **standing
regularity** of the framework: $F$ is continuous on $I_{0}\times Q\times
\mathbb R$ and locally Lipschitz in the state variable $(x,v)$ locally
uniformly in time ([[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]). The
framework's three-dimensional force branch is
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]]; the class declared here is a **restricted
model class** adopted at the same primitive level, in which the physical
position of a single label along one coordinate is the whole state. A model
whose force law fails the standing regularity is not a one-dimensional model
of this class. When a statement differentiates the force law or the potential,
the additional smoothness it needs is stated in that statement.

**(b) Motions.** Let $J\subseteq I_{0}$ be an interval with nonempty interior
(endpoints read with one-sided derivatives, as in
[[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]). A **motion** of
the model on $J$ is a curve $x:J\to Q$ of class $C^{2}$
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]) with
$$m\,x''(t)=F\bigl(t,x(t),x'(t)\bigr)\qquad(t\in J).$$
In the notation of the three-dimensional branch this is the scalar
restriction of its equation of motion clause (iv) to a single coordinate; the
motions of the present class are declared to be these curves. A **datum** at
time $t_{0}\in I_{0}$ is a triple $(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})$ with $x_{0}\in Q$ and
$v_{0}\in\mathbb R$; a motion $x$ **takes** the datum when $x(t_{0})=x_{0}$
and $x'(t_{0})=v_{0}$.

**(c) Phase system.** The **phase system** of the model is the first-order
system on the open set $I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R\subseteq\mathbb R^{3}$
with right-hand side
$$G_{F}(t,x,v):=\Bigl(v,\ \frac{F(t,x,v)}{m}\Bigr),$$
read as a system of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]];
its state variable is $z=(x,v)$. For an interval $J\subseteq I_0$ with
nonempty interior, a **phase solution** on $J$ means a differentiable curve
$z:J\to Q\times\mathbb R$ satisfying $z'(t)=G_F(t,z(t))$ for every $t\in J$,
with domain-relative derivatives at included endpoints. Equivalently, for
any $t_0\in J$ it is a solution in the cited IVP sense with datum
$(t_0,z(t_0))$. For a $C^2$ curve $x:J\to Q$, being a motion is equivalent
to $t\mapsto(x(t),x'(t))$ being a phase solution: the first component is
$x'=v$ and the second is $x''=F(t,x,x')/m$. Conversely a phase solution
$(x,v)$ has $x'=v$ and $v'=F(t,x,v)/m$; continuity of $F$ makes $v'$ continuous,
so $x$ is $C^2$ and is a motion. This is the argument of clause (c) of
[[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]] read in one
coordinate. Here $x$ is the **position** or **displacement** coordinate and
$v$ the **velocity** coordinate; both are read in the fixed inertial frame in
which the model is declared. The phase system inherits the standing
regularity: $G_{F}$ is continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable
locally uniformly in time, so the Picard–Lindelöf hypotheses of
[[thm-picard-lindelof-local-existence-and-uniqueness]] hold at every point of
its domain.

**(d) Potential presentation, residual forces and energy.** The model
**presents its force law through a potential** when it declares a function
$U:Q\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^{2}$ in the sense of clause (a) of
[[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]] of dimension
$\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$, read in joules, and a **residual force**
$d:I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ of the standing regularity of
(a), with
$$F(t,x,v)=-U'(x)+d(t,x,v)\qquad\bigl((t,x,v)\in I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R\bigr);$$
here $U'$ is the ordinary derivative. This is the one-coordinate case of the
potential presentation of [[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]] clause
(a) for a time- and velocity-independent potential, and the scalar
$U$ is a **potential energy** of the model's potential part. The model is a
**global potential model** (equivalently, in the framework's usage, a
**conservative model**) when $d\equiv0$; the term "conservative" is used only
in this sense, as recorded in that definition. For a conservative model the
**mechanical energy** is the function
$$E:Q\times\mathbb R\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad E(x,v):=\tfrac12 m v^{2}+U(x),$$
of dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$. For a model with declared residual
forces, the **mechanical energy along a motion** $x:J\to Q$ is
$E(t):=\tfrac12m\,x'(t)^{2}+U(x(t))$; it is defined along curve families even
though the force law is not presented through $U$ alone.

**(e) Equilibria.** A **time- and velocity-independent force law** on $Q$ is
one of the form $F(t,x,v)=f(x)$ for a function $f:Q\to\mathbb R$; the model
is then **autonomous**. For such a law, a point $x_{*}\in Q$ is an
**equilibrium** (or **rest position**) when $f(x_{*})=0$, and the phase-plane
point $(x_{*},0)$ is the corresponding **rest point** of the phase system;
the constant curve $x\equiv x_{*}$ is then a motion. When the force law is
presented as $f=-U'$ with $U$ of class $C^{2}$, the equilibria are exactly
the critical points of $U$:
$f(x_{*})=0\iff U'(x_{*})=0$. A point $x_{0}\in Q$ is a **strict local
minimum** of $U$ when $U(x)>U(x_{0})$ for every $x\in Q$ with $0<\lvert
x-x_{0}\rvert<r_{0}$ for some $r_{0}>0$. The **Lyapunov stability** and
**asymptotic stability** of a rest point of the autonomous phase system are
the notions of [[def-cm-equilibrium-and-lyapunov-stability]] applied to the
field $G_{F}$; they are not defined here anew.

**(f) Oscillator-type data.** Let $m>0$, $c\ge0$, $k\in\mathbb R$ and let
$f:I_{0}\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. A model **is of oscillator type with
data $(m,c,k,f)$** when its force law has the form
$$F(t,x,v)=f(t)-c\,v-k\,x\qquad\bigl((t,x,v)\in I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R\bigr)$$
with $Q$ a nonempty open interval containing $0$ when the equation is read
about the origin, and the parameters are read with dimensions $[c]=\mu\tau^{-1}$
(kilograms per second), $[k]=\mu\tau^{-2}$ (kilograms per second squared) and
$[f]=\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$ (newtons). For such a model the equation of motion is
the second-order equation $m\,x''+c\,x'+k\,x=f(t)$, and the motions are
exactly the restrictions of the solutions of the mathematical model of
[[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]] with the same data, by the
identification of that definition's phase system with the phase system (c).
The parameters $c$ and $k$ are model data: they enter the model's declaration
and are not derived by this item.

**(g) Status.** This item introduces vocabulary, objects, regularity and
dimensions; it contains no existence, uniqueness, conservation, stability or
boundedness assertion, no force law of nature and no measured value. In
particular, clause (a) **declares** the one-dimensional class rather than
deriving it from the three-dimensional branch, and clauses (d)-(f) only fix
which data a model of the class carries. Every later statement of this page
names the model data, the potential representative and the initial datum it
uses.

Adopt the damped oscillator model of [[post-cm04-linear-damping-model]] with
$m>0$, $k>0$, $c\ge0$, force law $F(x,v)=-kx-cv$ and mechanical energy
$E(x,v)=\tfrac12mv^{2}+\tfrac12kx^{2}$. Write
$$\Delta:=c^{2}-4mk,\qquad \gamma:=\frac{c}{2m},\qquad \lambda_{\pm}:=\frac{-c\pm\sqrt{\Delta}}{2m}\ (\Delta\ge0),\qquad \omega:=\frac{\sqrt{4mk-c^{2}}}{2m}\ (\Delta<0),$$
and note that $\Delta=-4mk<0$ and $\omega=\sqrt{k/m}$ when $c=0$. Then:

1. **Classification and uniqueness.** Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an
   interval with nonempty interior. A curve $x:J\to\mathbb R$ is a motion of
   the model if and only if it is one of the following:
   - $\Delta>0$: $x(t)=Ae^{\lambda_{+}t}+Be^{\lambda_{-}t}$ for reals $A,B$;
   - $\Delta=0$: $x(t)=(A+Bt)e^{-ct/(2m)}$ for reals $A,B$;
   - $\Delta<0$: $x(t)=e^{-\gamma t}\bigl(A\cos(\omega t)+B\sin(\omega
     t)\bigr)$ for reals $A,B$.
   For every datum $(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})$ there is exactly one maximal motion,
   it is defined on all of $\mathbb R$, and every motion with that datum is
   its restriction; when its family is written in $s=t-t_0$ instead of $t$, the coefficients
   are those supplied by clause 4 of
   [[thm-cm-homogeneous-oscillator-solution-classification]] for the shifted
   curve $s\mapsto x(t_{0}+s)$.
   In particular, for $c=0$ the motions are exactly those of the harmonic
   model of [[post-cm04-harmonic-model]] with the same $m$ and $k$.
2. **Energy dissipation.** For every motion $x:J\to\mathbb R$ the energy
   $e(t):=E(x(t),x'(t))$ is differentiable at every interior point of $J$
   with
   $$e'(t)=-c\,x'(t)^{2}\le0,$$
   and for $t_{1}<t_{2}$ in $J$ one has
   $e(t_{2})-e(t_{1})=-c\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}x'(s)^{2}\,ds\le0$: the energy is
   nonincreasing on $J$. If $c>0$, then the following are equivalent: (i)
   $e$ is constant on $J$; (ii) $x'(t)=0$ at every interior point of $J$;
   (iii) $x$ is constant on $J$; (iv) $x\equiv0$ on $J$, the rest motion of
   the model. Moreover, at every interior point with $x'(t)\neq0$ one has
   $e'(t)<0$, so the energy strictly decreases there.
3. **Rest points.** The rest points of the model are exactly the pairs
   $(x,0)$ with $kx=0$, that is $(0,0)$, and the constant curve $x\equiv0$ is
   its maximal motion with datum $(t_{0},0,0)$.

The statement is read for the declared data; it asserts no value of $m,k,c$
and no empirical decay law.

Let $m>0$, $c\ge0$ and $k>0$, and consider the homogeneous damped oscillator model $m\,x''+c\,x'+k\,x=0$ of [[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]] with time domain $I=\mathbb R$ and forcing $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ identically zero, with characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda)=m\lambda^2+c\lambda+k$, discriminant $\Delta=c^2-4mk$, damping rate $\gamma:=c/(2m)$, and, when applicable, roots
$$\lambda_\pm:=\frac{-c\pm\sqrt\Delta}{2m}\ (\Delta\ge0),\qquad \lambda:=-\frac{c}{2m},\qquad \omega:=\frac{\sqrt{4mk-c^2}}{2m}\ (\Delta<0).$$

A local solution here may have any interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ with nonempty interior, with domain-relative derivatives at included endpoints. It has a unique extension to the global family below. A **maximal solution** means one that has no solution extension to a strictly larger interval; the maximal solutions of this global autonomous equation are precisely the family members on $\mathbb R$. For a homogeneous model restricted to a time domain $I$, its solutions have $J\subseteq I$ and are restrictions of these same global members; their extensions solve the all-$\mathbb R$ equation.

1. **Distinct real roots.** If $\Delta>0$, then $\lambda_+>\lambda_-$ are exactly the real roots of $p$, and a function $x:J\to\mathbb R$ on an interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ with nonempty interior is a solution of the model if and only if
$$x(t)=Ae^{\lambda_+t}+Be^{\lambda_-t}\quad(t\in J)$$
for some $A,B\in\mathbb R$.

2. **Double real root.** If $\Delta=0$, then $\lambda=-c/(2m)$ is the only root of $p$, and $x:J\to\mathbb R$ is a solution if and only if
$$x(t)=(A+Bt)e^{\lambda t}\quad(t\in J)$$
for some $A,B\in\mathbb R$.

3. **Complex conjugate roots.** If $\Delta<0$, then $\omega>0$, the roots of $p$ are $-\gamma\pm i\omega$, and $x:J\to\mathbb R$ is a solution if and only if
$$x(t)=e^{-\gamma t}\bigl(A\cos(\omega t)+B\sin(\omega t)\bigr)\quad(t\in J)$$
for some $A,B\in\mathbb R$.

4. **Initial data.** In each of the three cases and for every $(x_0,v_0)\in\mathbb R^2$ there is exactly one solution $x:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ with $x(0)=x_0$ and $x'(0)=v_0$. Its coefficients are
$$A=\frac{v_0-\lambda_-x_0}{\lambda_+-\lambda_-},\quad B=\frac{\lambda_+x_0-v_0}{\lambda_+-\lambda_-}\quad(\Delta>0),\qquad A=x_0,\ B=v_0-\lambda x_0\quad(\Delta=0),$$
$$A=x_0,\quad B=\frac{v_0+\gamma x_0}{\omega}\quad(\Delta<0).$$

Let $m>0$, $c\ge0$ and $k\in\mathbb R$ be given real numbers, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $f:I\to\mathbb R$ be continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). The **damped driven oscillator model** with data $(m,c,k,f)$ is the second-order equation

$$m\,x''(t)+c\,x'(t)+k\,x(t)=f(t),\qquad t\in I .$$

A **solution** of the model on an interval $J\subseteq I$ with nonempty interior is a twice differentiable $x:J\to\mathbb R$ such that the identity holds for every $t\in J$, derivatives being ordinary real derivatives ([[def-derivative]], [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). The model is called **homogeneous** when $f\equiv 0$, **undamped** when $c=0$, and **strictly damped** when $c>0$.

The **phase-plane equation** of the model has right-hand side

$$G_f:I\times\mathbb R^2\longrightarrow\mathbb R^2,\qquad G_f(t,x,v):=\Bigl(v,\ \frac{f(t)-c\,v-k\,x}{m}\Bigr).$$

Here $\mathbb R^2$ is the **phase plane**, with coordinates $(x,v)$, where $x$ is the **displacement** and $v$ the **velocity**. For an interval $J\subseteq I$ with nonempty interior, a differentiable curve $z=(x,v):J\to\mathbb R^2$ solves the phase-plane equation when $z'(t)=G_f(t,z(t))$ for every $t\in J$, using the domain-relative derivative at any included endpoint ([[def-derivative]]). If $x$ is a solution of the model on $J$, then $t\mapsto(x(t),x'(t))$ solves this equation; conversely, if $t\mapsto(x(t),v(t))$ solves it, then $v=x'$ and $x$ is a solution of the model on $J$. When $J$ is open, this is the first-order system of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]] on the open domain $J\times\mathbb R^2$. For the homogeneous model the right-hand side is written $G_0(x,v)=(v,-(cv+kx)/m)$.

The **characteristic polynomial** of the model is

$$p(\lambda):=m\lambda^2+c\lambda+k,$$

with **discriminant** $\Delta:=c^2-4mk$. When $k>0$ define the **undamped frequency** $\omega_0:=\sqrt{k/m}$, the **damping rate** $\gamma:=c/(2m)$ and, when $4mk>c^2$, the **damped frequency** $\omega:=\sqrt{k/m-\gamma^2}=\sqrt{4mk-c^2}/(2m)$; the corresponding square roots are the nonnegative real ones.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

$$\exp(x)\to+\infty\quad(x\to+\infty),\qquad \exp(x)\to0\quad(x\to-\infty),$$
and the range of $\exp$ is contained in $(0,\infty)$ and is unbounded above with infimum $0$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

Let $(a_k)$ be a sequence of reals with $a_k \ge 0$ for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$,
let $s_n = \sum_{k<n} a_k$ be its partial sums and let
$S = \{\, s_n : n \in \mathbb{N} \,\}$ be the range of $(s_n)$ ([[def-series]]).
Then:

1. $(s_n)$ is nondecreasing ([[def-monotone-sequence]]) and $s_n \ge 0$ for every
   $n$;
2. $\sum a_k$ converges **if and only if** $S$ is bounded above
   ([[def-bounded-set]]), and in that case
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k \;=\; \sup S ,$$
   so in particular $s_n \le \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k$ for every $n$;
3. if $S$ is not bounded above then $s_n \to +\infty$
   ([[def-divergence-to-infinity]]) and $\sum a_k$ diverges.

This is the theorem that makes the nonnegative theory work: for terms of one
sign, convergence is a boundedness question and no candidate limit is ever
needed. Every comparison test on this page is an application of it.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field. For $a, b \ge 0$:

$$a < b \iff a^2 < b^2, \qquad a \le b \iff a^2 \le b^2.$$

More generally, for arbitrary $a, b \in F$, $a^2 < b^2 \iff |a| < |b|$.

derivations.claim: Preliminary. Because the phase system is autonomous, all statements are invariant under translating time, and it suffices to consider the datum at $t_{0}=0$; the functions $x$ and $x'$ of the statement are then defined for all $t\ge0$ by [L1]. Let $X_{0}:=x_{0}$ and $V_{0}:=v_{0}$ be the normalized numerical SI coordinates of the datum, and let $M,K$ be the dimensionless numerical values of $m,k$ defined in Given; then $r_{0}^{2}=X_{0}^{2}+V_{0}^{2}$. With $\mathcal E:=E/(1\,\mathrm J)$, the normalized initial energy is $$\mathcal E(0)=\tfrac12MV_{0}^{2}+\tfrac12KX_{0}^{2}\le\tfrac12\max(M,K)\,r_{0}^{2},$$ since $X_{0}^{2},V_{0}^{2}\le r_{0}^{2}$. By [L1] the energy is nonincreasing and $\mathcal E(t)\ge\tfrac12MV(t)^{2}$, where $V(t):=x'(t)$ is the normalized numerical SI velocity coordinate; hence $$\lvert V(t)\rvert\le\sqrt{\frac{2\mathcal E(t)}{M}}\le\sqrt{\frac{\max(M,K)}{M}}\;r_{0}\qquad(t\ge0).$$ This is the uniform normalized velocity bound with $C_{2}^{\mathrm E}:=\sqrt{\max(M,K)/M}$; and every maximal motion is defined on all of $\mathbb R$, while arbitrary local motions are its restrictions by [L1].

Case $\Delta>0$. Let $\Lambda_{\pm}:=(1\,\mathrm s)\lambda_{\pm}$ and $d:=\Lambda_{+}-\Lambda_{-}>0$ be the numerical SI rates and their difference. Write $\bar A,\bar B$ for the numerical SI values of the position coefficients $A,B$ in [L1]. Their formulas give $$\bar A=\frac{V_{0}-\Lambda_{-}X_{0}}{d},\qquad\bar B=\frac{\Lambda_{+}X_{0}-V_{0}}{d}.$$ Hence $|\bar A|\le(1+|\Lambda_{-}|)r_{0}/d$ and $|\bar B|\le(1+|\Lambda_{+}|)r_{0}/d$, since $|X_{0}|,|V_{0}|\le r_{0}$. By [L2], $|x(t)|\le(|\bar A|+|\bar B|)e^{\Lambda_{+}t}$, so $|x(t)|\le C_{1}r_{0}$ with $C_{1}:=(2+|\Lambda_{-}|+|\Lambda_{+}|)/d$, using $e^{\Lambda_{+}t}\le1$ for $t\ge0$ by [L3]. Differentiating $x(t)=\bar A e^{\Lambda_{+}t}+\bar B e^{\Lambda_{-}t}$ gives the numerical velocity $x'(t)=\Lambda_{+}\bar A e^{\Lambda_{+}t}+\Lambda_{-}\bar B e^{\Lambda_{-}t}$, so $|x'(t)|\le(|\Lambda_{+}||\bar A|+|\Lambda_{-}||\bar B|)e^{\Lambda_{+}t}$, the normalized form of the displayed case bound; it tends to $0$ because $e^{\Lambda_{+}t}\to0$ by [L3].

Case $\Delta=0$. Write $\Lambda:=(1\,\mathrm s)\lambda<0$, and let $\bar A,\bar B$ be the numerical SI values of the critical-case coefficients in [L1]. The coefficient formulas give $\bar A=X_{0}$ and $\bar B=V_{0}-\Lambda X_{0}$, so $|\bar A|\le r_{0}$ and $|\bar B|\le(1+|\Lambda|)r_{0}$. For $t\ge0$ put $u=|\Lambda|t\ge0$; by [L4], $u\le e^{u}$, so $t e^{\Lambda t}\le1/|\Lambda|$. By [L2], the normalized position satisfies $|x(t)|\le(|\bar A|+|\bar B|t)e^{\Lambda t}\le|\bar A|+|\bar B|/|\Lambda|\le(2+1/|\Lambda|)r_{0}$; take $C_{1}:=2+1/|\Lambda|$. For convergence use $t e^{-|\Lambda|t}\le(2/|\Lambda|)e^{-|\Lambda|t/2}$, obtained from [L4] with $u=|\Lambda|t/2$. Thus $|x(t)|\le|\bar A|e^{-|\Lambda|t}+(2|\bar B|/|\Lambda|)e^{-|\Lambda|t/2}\to0$ by [L3]. Differentiating $x(t)=(\bar A+\bar B t)e^{\Lambda t}$ gives the numerical velocity $x'(t)=(\Lambda\bar A+\bar B+\Lambda\bar B t)e^{\Lambda t}$; its $t$-term tends to $0$ by the same inequality and its other term tends to $0$ by [L3]. This proves the displayed case bounds and $x'(t)\to0$.

Case $\Delta<0$. Write $\Gamma:=(1\,\mathrm s)\gamma>0$ and $W:=(1\,\mathrm s)\omega>0$, and let $\bar A,\bar B$ be the numerical SI values of the oscillatory-case coefficients in [L1]. Then $\bar A=X_{0}$ and $\bar B=(V_{0}+\Gamma X_{0})/W$, so $|\bar A|\le r_{0}$ and $|\bar B|\le(1+\Gamma)r_{0}/W$. By [L2], the numerical position satisfies $|x(t)|\le(|\bar A|+|\bar B|)e^{-\Gamma t}$, which tends to $0$ by [L3]; take $C_{1}:=1+(1+\Gamma)/W$. Differentiating $x(t)=e^{-\Gamma t}(\bar A\cos(Wt)+\bar B\sin(Wt))$ gives the numerical velocity $$x'(t)=e^{-\Gamma t}\bigl[(W\bar B-\Gamma\bar A)\cos(Wt)-(\Gamma\bar B+W\bar A)\sin(Wt)\bigr],$$ so its absolute value is bounded by the normalized form of the displayed case bound and tends to $0$ by [L3].

Uniform bound and stability. By the three cases of steps 2.1-2.3 the numerical position bound $|x(t)|\le C_{1}r_{0}$ holds for all $t\ge0$ with the constant $C_{1}$ of the case at hand, and by step 1.1 the numerical velocity bound $|x'(t)|\le C_{2}r_{0}$ holds with the universal constant $C_{2}:=C_{2}^{\mathrm E}$ from energy monotonicity; both dimensionless constants depend only on the numerical SI values of $(m,k,c)$. Let $\varepsilon>0$ and set $\delta:=\varepsilon/(C_{1}+C_{2})>0$. If a maximal motion satisfies $r_{0}=\lVert(x(t_{0}),x'(t_{0}))\rVert_{2}<\delta$ for some $t_{0}$, then the shifted curve $s\mapsto x(t_{0}+s)$ is again a motion of the autonomous model, with datum $(0,x(t_{0}),x'(t_{0}))$ and the same initial phase norm $r_{0}$. Applying the uniform bounds of steps 1.1 and 2.1-2.3 gives $$\lVert(x(t),x'(t))\rVert_{2}=\sqrt{x(t)^{2}+x'(t)^{2}}\le|x(t)|+|x'(t)|\le(C_{1}+C_{2})r_{0}<\varepsilon\qquad(t\ge t_{0}),$$ where the norm is on the normalized SI phase coordinates of [[def-cm04-phase-plane-and-energy-level-sets]]. Thus $(0,0)$ is Lyapunov stable in the sense of [[def-cm-equilibrium-and-lyapunov-stability]]; and clauses 1 and 2 give $x(t)\to0$, $x'(t)\to0$ for every maximal motion, so every maximal motion tends to the rest point in the phase-plane norm and $(0,0)$ is globally asymptotically stable.

boundaries.reason: The statement fixes one strictly damped model and quantifies over its motions; no possibly empty family is quantified.

boundaries.evidence: Zero initial data give the rest motion, for which the bounds hold with r_0=0 and the stability conclusion is the equilibrium itself; the case r_0=0 is included in the bound of step 3.1.
The model is one-dimensional; the coefficient estimates of steps 2.1-2.3 are scalar and the phase norm is the Euclidean norm on R^2.
The double-root case Delta=0 is handled at step 2.2 with the factor t e^{lambda t}; the inequality u<=e^u of [L4] avoids any division by a vanishing quantity since c>0 gives lambda<0.
The decay and convergence statements are for t>=t_0; the bounds are established for t>=0 after the autonomous time shift of step 3.1, and no endpoint derivative is taken.

boundaries.reason: The argument estimates explicit coefficients and applies a fixed theorem; no selection is made.
The item asserts bounds, convergence and stability; it is not stated as an equivalence.
The Statement assumes strictly positive damping and derives decay and asymptotic stability; it gives no converse asserting that all asymptotically stable systems have this oscillator force law.

risk_review.notes:
Checked six steps in three regimes, including zero datum. SI-normalized M,K prevent comparisons of unlike dimensions; energy gives C2=sqrt(max(M,K)/M). Distinct-root gap positive and roots negative; repeated-root rate nonzero and t exp(lambda t) bounded and decays via u<=exp(u); oscillatory W>0 and Gamma>0. Coefficient constants finite for each fixed parameter triple. Uniform norm bound with delta=epsilon/(C1+C2), autonomy and global classification establish global asymptotic stability; c=0 excluded.

Focused owner review of changed oscillator public-domain supplier and actual affected use: Statement is about x:R/maximal motions; proof1.1 explicitly distinguishes local restrictions. Negative discriminant rates, critical polynomial factor and phase norm constants continue to apply; no change to physical scope or units. Durable consumer disposition: research/physics-cm-qm-gr-79-2026-10-11-owner-oscillator-domain/consumer-dispositions.json.

citations.quote:
**(i) Setting.** Work in the one-dimensional model class of
[[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]] with time window
$I_{0}=\mathbb R$, configuration domain $Q=\mathbb R$, mass $m>0$, spring
constant $k>0$ ([[post-cm04-harmonic-model]]) and drag coefficient $c\ge0$
([[post-cm04-linear-damping-model]]). Let a real **drive amplitude**
$f_{0}\in\mathbb R$ of dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$ (newtons) and an
**angular drive frequency** $\Omega>0$ of dimension $\tau^{-1}$ (radians per
second; the radian is dimensionless in the framework's angle convention,
[[def-cm01-units]]) be declared. Adopt, through the additive composition of
force contributions of clause (v) of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] and
the external-contribution reading of [[post-cm02-interactions]], the force
law
$$F(t,x,v):=f_{0}\cos(\Omega t)-k\,x-c\,v .$$
The **sinusoidally driven oscillator model** is the one-dimensional model
with this force law; its equation of motion is
$$m\,x''+c\,x'+k\,x=f_{0}\cos(\Omega t),$$
and its data $(m,c,k,f)$ with $f(t)=f_{0}\cos(\Omega t)$ are oscillator-type
data in the sense of clause (f) of
[[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]]. The term
$f_{0}\cos(\Omega t)$ is the **drive** or **driving force**; the model is
undamped when $c=0$ and strictly damped when $c>0$.

**(ii) The drive is prescribed external data.** The driving force is a
prescribed function of time alone: it does not depend on $x$ or on $x'$, and
the object producing it is not one of the model's labels and is not modelled
dynamically. This is the same modelling status as the medium of
[[post-cm02-drag]]: the drive is an external contribution declared as part
of the model. A real apparatus, background or force generator that reacts to
the motion is **not** represented by this model; representing such a
back-reaction requires a larger model with additional states.

**(iii) Potential presentation with residual force.** The model presents its
force law through the harmonic potential $U(x)=\tfrac12kx^{2}$ with residual
force $d(t,x,v)=f_{0}\cos(\Omega t)-c\,v$, in the sense of clause (d) of
[[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]]:
$F(t,x,v)=-U'(x)+d(t,x,v)$. The mechanical energy of the model is
$E(x,v)=\tfrac12mv^{2}+\tfrac12kx^{2}$ of that clause, defined along every
motion; the model is driven and not a global potential model whenever
$f_{0}\neq0$.

**(iv) Regularity.** Let $X:=x_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm m)$,
$V:=v_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm{m/s})$, and $T:=t_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm s)$
be the dimensionless numerical SI coordinates (the real inputs of the force
map). Write
$K:=k_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm{N/m})$,
$C:=c_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm{kg/s})$,
$\widehat f_{0}:=f_{0}/(1\,\mathrm N)$, and
$\widehat\Omega:=\Omega(1\,\mathrm s)$. The numerical force map is
$$\widehat F(T,X,V)=\widehat f_{0}\cos(\widehat\Omega T)-KX-CV,$$
so it is continuous and globally Lipschitz in the state variable with
numerical-coordinate constant $K+C$, uniformly in time. This is a bound on
dimensionless SI coordinates and force values, not a sum of the dimensionful
$k$ and $c$ ([[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]). It is an
admissible force law of clause (a) of [[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]],
and its equation is the forced model $m\,x''+cx'+kx=f$ of
[[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]] with the continuous function
$f(t)=f_{0}\cos(\Omega t)$.

**(v) Physical status and regime.** The model is a **restricted idealization**
adopted rather than derived: exactly sinusoidal, with constant amplitude and
frequency and no dependence on the motion. The drive amplitude and frequency
are model parameters; when their values come from an apparatus calibration,
that use is an empirical premise carrying the apparatus conditions and the
measurement uncertainty, and this item asserts no such value. The sinusoidal
form is the elementary component used by the recorded treatments; the
response to a non-sinusoidal periodic drive is a superposition statement
belonging to the mathematical theory, not an additional claim here. The
model's undamped case $c=0$ is included as a parameter value, and it is where
the resonant unboundedness of the following theorem occurs.

**(vi) Status.** Adopted assumption of the framework when a model invokes
it; it selects no law of nature on its own, and no measured response, no
resonance curve of any apparatus and no empirical resonance phenomenon is
asserted by the postulate.

**(a) Data of a one-dimensional model.** A **one-dimensional model** is
declared by the following data: a fixed positive **mass** $m>0$, of dimension
$\mu$ read in kilograms ([[def-cm01-units]], [[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause
(v)); a **time window** $I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$, a nondegenerate open
interval read in seconds ([[def-interval]]); an open **configuration
domain** $Q\subseteq\mathbb R$, a nonempty open interval of the real line
read in metres; and a **force law**
$$F:I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad (t,x,v)\longmapsto F(t,x,v),$$
of dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$, read in newtons, subject to the **standing
regularity** of the framework: $F$ is continuous on $I_{0}\times Q\times
\mathbb R$ and locally Lipschitz in the state variable $(x,v)$ locally
uniformly in time ([[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]). The
framework's three-dimensional force branch is
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]]; the class declared here is a **restricted
model class** adopted at the same primitive level, in which the physical
position of a single label along one coordinate is the whole state. A model
whose force law fails the standing regularity is not a one-dimensional model
of this class. When a statement differentiates the force law or the potential,
the additional smoothness it needs is stated in that statement.

**(b) Motions.** Let $J\subseteq I_{0}$ be an interval with nonempty interior
(endpoints read with one-sided derivatives, as in
[[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]). A **motion** of
the model on $J$ is a curve $x:J\to Q$ of class $C^{2}$
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]) with
$$m\,x''(t)=F\bigl(t,x(t),x'(t)\bigr)\qquad(t\in J).$$
In the notation of the three-dimensional branch this is the scalar
restriction of its equation of motion clause (iv) to a single coordinate; the
motions of the present class are declared to be these curves. A **datum** at
time $t_{0}\in I_{0}$ is a triple $(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})$ with $x_{0}\in Q$ and
$v_{0}\in\mathbb R$; a motion $x$ **takes** the datum when $x(t_{0})=x_{0}$
and $x'(t_{0})=v_{0}$.

**(c) Phase system.** The **phase system** of the model is the first-order
system on the open set $I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R\subseteq\mathbb R^{3}$
with right-hand side
$$G_{F}(t,x,v):=\Bigl(v,\ \frac{F(t,x,v)}{m}\Bigr),$$
read as a system of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]];
its state variable is $z=(x,v)$. For an interval $J\subseteq I_0$ with
nonempty interior, a **phase solution** on $J$ means a differentiable curve
$z:J\to Q\times\mathbb R$ satisfying $z'(t)=G_F(t,z(t))$ for every $t\in J$,
with domain-relative derivatives at included endpoints. Equivalently, for
any $t_0\in J$ it is a solution in the cited IVP sense with datum
$(t_0,z(t_0))$. For a $C^2$ curve $x:J\to Q$, being a motion is equivalent
to $t\mapsto(x(t),x'(t))$ being a phase solution: the first component is
$x'=v$ and the second is $x''=F(t,x,x')/m$. Conversely a phase solution
$(x,v)$ has $x'=v$ and $v'=F(t,x,v)/m$; continuity of $F$ makes $v'$ continuous,
so $x$ is $C^2$ and is a motion. This is the argument of clause (c) of
[[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]] read in one
coordinate. Here $x$ is the **position** or **displacement** coordinate and
$v$ the **velocity** coordinate; both are read in the fixed inertial frame in
which the model is declared. The phase system inherits the standing
regularity: $G_{F}$ is continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable
locally uniformly in time, so the Picard–Lindelöf hypotheses of
[[thm-picard-lindelof-local-existence-and-uniqueness]] hold at every point of
its domain.

**(d) Potential presentation, residual forces and energy.** The model
**presents its force law through a potential** when it declares a function
$U:Q\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^{2}$ in the sense of clause (a) of
[[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]] of dimension
$\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$, read in joules, and a **residual force**
$d:I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ of the standing regularity of
(a), with
$$F(t,x,v)=-U'(x)+d(t,x,v)\qquad\bigl((t,x,v)\in I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R\bigr);$$
here $U'$ is the ordinary derivative. This is the one-coordinate case of the
potential presentation of [[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]] clause
(a) for a time- and velocity-independent potential, and the scalar
$U$ is a **potential energy** of the model's potential part. The model is a
**global potential model** (equivalently, in the framework's usage, a
**conservative model**) when $d\equiv0$; the term "conservative" is used only
in this sense, as recorded in that definition. For a conservative model the
**mechanical energy** is the function
$$E:Q\times\mathbb R\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad E(x,v):=\tfrac12 m v^{2}+U(x),$$
of dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$. For a model with declared residual
forces, the **mechanical energy along a motion** $x:J\to Q$ is
$E(t):=\tfrac12m\,x'(t)^{2}+U(x(t))$; it is defined along curve families even
though the force law is not presented through $U$ alone.

**(e) Equilibria.** A **time- and velocity-independent force law** on $Q$ is
one of the form $F(t,x,v)=f(x)$ for a function $f:Q\to\mathbb R$; the model
is then **autonomous**. For such a law, a point $x_{*}\in Q$ is an
**equilibrium** (or **rest position**) when $f(x_{*})=0$, and the phase-plane
point $(x_{*},0)$ is the corresponding **rest point** of the phase system;
the constant curve $x\equiv x_{*}$ is then a motion. When the force law is
presented as $f=-U'$ with $U$ of class $C^{2}$, the equilibria are exactly
the critical points of $U$:
$f(x_{*})=0\iff U'(x_{*})=0$. A point $x_{0}\in Q$ is a **strict local
minimum** of $U$ when $U(x)>U(x_{0})$ for every $x\in Q$ with $0<\lvert
x-x_{0}\rvert<r_{0}$ for some $r_{0}>0$. The **Lyapunov stability** and
**asymptotic stability** of a rest point of the autonomous phase system are
the notions of [[def-cm-equilibrium-and-lyapunov-stability]] applied to the
field $G_{F}$; they are not defined here anew.

**(f) Oscillator-type data.** Let $m>0$, $c\ge0$, $k\in\mathbb R$ and let
$f:I_{0}\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. A model **is of oscillator type with
data $(m,c,k,f)$** when its force law has the form
$$F(t,x,v)=f(t)-c\,v-k\,x\qquad\bigl((t,x,v)\in I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R\bigr)$$
with $Q$ a nonempty open interval containing $0$ when the equation is read
about the origin, and the parameters are read with dimensions $[c]=\mu\tau^{-1}$
(kilograms per second), $[k]=\mu\tau^{-2}$ (kilograms per second squared) and
$[f]=\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$ (newtons). For such a model the equation of motion is
the second-order equation $m\,x''+c\,x'+k\,x=f(t)$, and the motions are
exactly the restrictions of the solutions of the mathematical model of
[[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]] with the same data, by the
identification of that definition's phase system with the phase system (c).
The parameters $c$ and $k$ are model data: they enter the model's declaration
and are not derived by this item.

**(g) Status.** This item introduces vocabulary, objects, regularity and
dimensions; it contains no existence, uniqueness, conservation, stability or
boundedness assertion, no force law of nature and no measured value. In
particular, clause (a) **declares** the one-dimensional class rather than
deriving it from the three-dimensional branch, and clauses (d)-(f) only fix
which data a model of the class carries. Every later statement of this page
names the model data, the potential representative and the initial datum it
uses.

Let $m>0$, $c\ge0$ and $k\in\mathbb R$ be given real numbers, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $f:I\to\mathbb R$ be continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). The **damped driven oscillator model** with data $(m,c,k,f)$ is the second-order equation

$$m\,x''(t)+c\,x'(t)+k\,x(t)=f(t),\qquad t\in I .$$

A **solution** of the model on an interval $J\subseteq I$ with nonempty interior is a twice differentiable $x:J\to\mathbb R$ such that the identity holds for every $t\in J$, derivatives being ordinary real derivatives ([[def-derivative]], [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). The model is called **homogeneous** when $f\equiv 0$, **undamped** when $c=0$, and **strictly damped** when $c>0$.

The **phase-plane equation** of the model has right-hand side

$$G_f:I\times\mathbb R^2\longrightarrow\mathbb R^2,\qquad G_f(t,x,v):=\Bigl(v,\ \frac{f(t)-c\,v-k\,x}{m}\Bigr).$$

Here $\mathbb R^2$ is the **phase plane**, with coordinates $(x,v)$, where $x$ is the **displacement** and $v$ the **velocity**. For an interval $J\subseteq I$ with nonempty interior, a differentiable curve $z=(x,v):J\to\mathbb R^2$ solves the phase-plane equation when $z'(t)=G_f(t,z(t))$ for every $t\in J$, using the domain-relative derivative at any included endpoint ([[def-derivative]]). If $x$ is a solution of the model on $J$, then $t\mapsto(x(t),x'(t))$ solves this equation; conversely, if $t\mapsto(x(t),v(t))$ solves it, then $v=x'$ and $x$ is a solution of the model on $J$. When $J$ is open, this is the first-order system of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]] on the open domain $J\times\mathbb R^2$. For the homogeneous model the right-hand side is written $G_0(x,v)=(v,-(cv+kx)/m)$.

The **characteristic polynomial** of the model is

$$p(\lambda):=m\lambda^2+c\lambda+k,$$

with **discriminant** $\Delta:=c^2-4mk$. When $k>0$ define the **undamped frequency** $\omega_0:=\sqrt{k/m}$, the **damping rate** $\gamma:=c/(2m)$ and, when $4mk>c^2$, the **damped frequency** $\omega:=\sqrt{k/m-\gamma^2}=\sqrt{4mk-c^2}/(2m)$; the corresponding square roots are the nonnegative real ones.

Adopt the damped oscillator model of [[post-cm04-linear-damping-model]] with
$m>0$, $k>0$, $c\ge0$, force law $F(x,v)=-kx-cv$ and mechanical energy
$E(x,v)=\tfrac12mv^{2}+\tfrac12kx^{2}$. Write
$$\Delta:=c^{2}-4mk,\qquad \gamma:=\frac{c}{2m},\qquad \lambda_{\pm}:=\frac{-c\pm\sqrt{\Delta}}{2m}\ (\Delta\ge0),\qquad \omega:=\frac{\sqrt{4mk-c^{2}}}{2m}\ (\Delta<0),$$
and note that $\Delta=-4mk<0$ and $\omega=\sqrt{k/m}$ when $c=0$. Then:

1. **Classification and uniqueness.** Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an
   interval with nonempty interior. A curve $x:J\to\mathbb R$ is a motion of
   the model if and only if it is one of the following:
   - $\Delta>0$: $x(t)=Ae^{\lambda_{+}t}+Be^{\lambda_{-}t}$ for reals $A,B$;
   - $\Delta=0$: $x(t)=(A+Bt)e^{-ct/(2m)}$ for reals $A,B$;
   - $\Delta<0$: $x(t)=e^{-\gamma t}\bigl(A\cos(\omega t)+B\sin(\omega
     t)\bigr)$ for reals $A,B$.
   For every datum $(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})$ there is exactly one maximal motion,
   it is defined on all of $\mathbb R$, and every motion with that datum is
   its restriction; when its family is written in $s=t-t_0$ instead of $t$, the coefficients
   are those supplied by clause 4 of
   [[thm-cm-homogeneous-oscillator-solution-classification]] for the shifted
   curve $s\mapsto x(t_{0}+s)$.
   In particular, for $c=0$ the motions are exactly those of the harmonic
   model of [[post-cm04-harmonic-model]] with the same $m$ and $k$.
2. **Energy dissipation.** For every motion $x:J\to\mathbb R$ the energy
   $e(t):=E(x(t),x'(t))$ is differentiable at every interior point of $J$
   with
   $$e'(t)=-c\,x'(t)^{2}\le0,$$
   and for $t_{1}<t_{2}$ in $J$ one has
   $e(t_{2})-e(t_{1})=-c\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}x'(s)^{2}\,ds\le0$: the energy is
   nonincreasing on $J$. If $c>0$, then the following are equivalent: (i)
   $e$ is constant on $J$; (ii) $x'(t)=0$ at every interior point of $J$;
   (iii) $x$ is constant on $J$; (iv) $x\equiv0$ on $J$, the rest motion of
   the model. Moreover, at every interior point with $x'(t)\neq0$ one has
   $e'(t)<0$, so the energy strictly decreases there.
3. **Rest points.** The rest points of the model are exactly the pairs
   $(x,0)$ with $kx=0$, that is $(0,0)$, and the constant curve $x\equiv0$ is
   its maximal motion with datum $(t_{0},0,0)$.

The statement is read for the declared data; it asserts no value of $m,k,c$
and no empirical decay law.

Let $m>0$, $k>0$, $c\ge0$, let $f_0\in\mathbb R$ and $\Omega\ge0$, and consider the forced model $m\,x''+c\,x'+k\,x=f$ with time domain $I=\mathbb R$ and forcing $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, $f(t)=f_0\cos(\Omega t)$ ([[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]]). Put

$$D:=k-m\Omega^2+i\,c\,\Omega\in\mathbb C,\qquad \omega_0:=\sqrt{k/m}.$$

1. **Non-resonant response.** If $D\ne0$, then the function
$$x_p(t):=\operatorname{Re}\!\left(\frac{f_0e^{i\Omega t}}{D}\right)=f_0\,\frac{(k-m\Omega^2)\cos(\Omega t)+c\,\Omega\sin(\Omega t)}{(k-m\Omega^2)^2+c^2\Omega^2}$$
is a solution of the forced model on all of $\mathbb R$. Its amplitude about zero is $|f_0|/\sqrt{(k-m\Omega^2)^2+c^2\Omega^2}$. For $\Omega>0$ and $f_0\ne0$, a **phase-lag angle relative to the drive** means a real $\phi$ such that $x_p(t)=(f_0/|D|)\cos(\Omega t-\phi)$ for every $t$, with the signed factor $f_0$ retained in both drive and response. Such an angle exists: any $\phi\in\mathbb R$ satisfying
$$\cos\phi=\frac{k-m\Omega^2}{|D|},\qquad\sin\phi=\frac{c\Omega}{|D|}$$
has this property. No temporal phase is assigned when $\Omega=0$ or $f_0=0$.

2. **Resonance.** If $c=0$ and $\Omega=\omega_0$, then $D=0$ and
$$x_p(t):=\frac{f_0\,t\sin(\omega_0t)}{2m\omega_0}$$
is a solution of the forced model on all of $\mathbb R$; if $f_0\ne0$ then $x_p$ is unbounded on $[0,\infty)$.

3. **Transient decay.** If $c>0$, then $D\ne0$ for every $\Omega\ge0$, and every solution $x:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ of the forced model satisfies
$$x(t)=x_p(t)+x_h(t)$$
where $x_h$ is a homogeneous solution; consequently $x(t)-x_p(t)\to0$ as $t\to+\infty$ ([[def-limits-at-infinity]]) and $x$ is bounded on $[0,\infty)$.

Let $m>0$, $c\ge0$, $k\ge0$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $f:I\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. Fix $t_0\in I$ and data $(x_0,v_0)\in\mathbb R^2$. Let $g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be the (unique) solution of the associated homogeneous model with time domain $\mathbb R$ and zero forcing, with $g(0)=0$ and $g'(0)=1/m$.

Then:

1. There is exactly one solution $x:I\to\mathbb R$ of the forced model $m\,x''+c\,x'+k\,x=f$ with $x(t_0)=x_0$ and $x'(t_0)=v_0$. It is twice differentiable on $I$, with derivatives at included endpoints taken relative to $I$, and $x''$ is continuous on $I$ in its relative topology.
2. If $x_h:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is any homogeneous solution with $x_h(t_0)=x_0$ and $x_h'(t_0)=v_0$ (it exists and is unique by [[thm-cm-homogeneous-oscillator-solution-classification]] and [[prop-cm-oscillator-degenerate-and-repulsive-cases]]), then
$$x(t)=x_h(t)+\int_{t_0}^tg(t-s)f(s)\,ds\qquad(t\in I).$$

Let $m>0$, $c\ge0$ and $k>0$, and consider the homogeneous damped oscillator model $m\,x''+c\,x'+k\,x=0$ of [[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]] with time domain $I=\mathbb R$ and forcing $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ identically zero, with characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda)=m\lambda^2+c\lambda+k$, discriminant $\Delta=c^2-4mk$, damping rate $\gamma:=c/(2m)$, and, when applicable, roots
$$\lambda_\pm:=\frac{-c\pm\sqrt\Delta}{2m}\ (\Delta\ge0),\qquad \lambda:=-\frac{c}{2m},\qquad \omega:=\frac{\sqrt{4mk-c^2}}{2m}\ (\Delta<0).$$

A local solution here may have any interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ with nonempty interior, with domain-relative derivatives at included endpoints. It has a unique extension to the global family below. A **maximal solution** means one that has no solution extension to a strictly larger interval; the maximal solutions of this global autonomous equation are precisely the family members on $\mathbb R$. For a homogeneous model restricted to a time domain $I$, its solutions have $J\subseteq I$ and are restrictions of these same global members; their extensions solve the all-$\mathbb R$ equation.

1. **Distinct real roots.** If $\Delta>0$, then $\lambda_+>\lambda_-$ are exactly the real roots of $p$, and a function $x:J\to\mathbb R$ on an interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ with nonempty interior is a solution of the model if and only if
$$x(t)=Ae^{\lambda_+t}+Be^{\lambda_-t}\quad(t\in J)$$
for some $A,B\in\mathbb R$.

2. **Double real root.** If $\Delta=0$, then $\lambda=-c/(2m)$ is the only root of $p$, and $x:J\to\mathbb R$ is a solution if and only if
$$x(t)=(A+Bt)e^{\lambda t}\quad(t\in J)$$
for some $A,B\in\mathbb R$.

3. **Complex conjugate roots.** If $\Delta<0$, then $\omega>0$, the roots of $p$ are $-\gamma\pm i\omega$, and $x:J\to\mathbb R$ is a solution if and only if
$$x(t)=e^{-\gamma t}\bigl(A\cos(\omega t)+B\sin(\omega t)\bigr)\quad(t\in J)$$
for some $A,B\in\mathbb R$.

4. **Initial data.** In each of the three cases and for every $(x_0,v_0)\in\mathbb R^2$ there is exactly one solution $x:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ with $x(0)=x_0$ and $x'(0)=v_0$. Its coefficients are
$$A=\frac{v_0-\lambda_-x_0}{\lambda_+-\lambda_-},\quad B=\frac{\lambda_+x_0-v_0}{\lambda_+-\lambda_-}\quad(\Delta>0),\qquad A=x_0,\ B=v_0-\lambda x_0\quad(\Delta=0),$$
$$A=x_0,\quad B=\frac{v_0+\gamma x_0}{\omega}\quad(\Delta<0).$$

Adopt the damped oscillator model of [[post-cm04-linear-damping-model]] with
$m>0$, $k>0$ and $c>0$ (strict damping), force law $F(x,v)=-kx-cv$ and
energy $E(x,v)=\tfrac12mv^{2}+\tfrac12kx^{2}$. Position and velocity
coordinates in every phase norm below are their normalized numerical SI
values, as defined in clause (a) of
[[def-cm04-phase-plane-and-energy-level-sets]]. For the datum
$(0,x_{0},v_{0})$, put $r_{0}:=\lVert(x_{0},v_{0})\rVert_{2}$ in that norm.
In displayed time-dependent formulas, $t$ is read numerically in seconds,
and rates in exponents are read in inverse seconds. Write
$\Delta=c^{2}-4mk$, $\gamma=c/(2m)>0$,
$\lambda_{\pm}=(-c\pm\sqrt{\Delta})/(2m)$ for $\Delta\ge0$,
$\lambda=-c/(2m)$ for $\Delta=0$ and $\omega=\sqrt{4mk-c^{2}}/(2m)$ for
$\Delta<0$. Then:

1. **Motion bounds.** For every motion $x:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ of the model
   with datum $(0,x_{0},v_{0})$ and phase norm $r_{0}$ the following bounds
   hold for all $t\ge0$, with the coefficients $A,B$ of the
   classification of [[pthm-cm04-damped-motion]]:
   - $\Delta>0$: $\lvert x(t)\rvert\le(\lvert A\rvert+\lvert
     B\rvert)e^{\lambda_{+}t}$ and
     $\lvert x'(t)\rvert\le\bigl(\lvert\lambda_{+}\rvert\lvert
     A\rvert+\lvert\lambda_{-}\rvert\lvert B\rvert\bigr)e^{\lambda_{+}t}$;
   - $\Delta=0$: $\lvert x(t)\rvert\le(\lvert A\rvert+\lvert
     B\rvert t)e^{\lambda t}$ and
     $\lvert x'(t)\rvert\le\bigl(\lvert\lambda A+B\rvert+\lvert\lambda
     B\rvert t\bigr)e^{\lambda t}$;
   - $\Delta<0$: $\lvert x(t)\rvert\le(\lvert A\rvert+\lvert
     B\rvert)e^{-\gamma t}$ and $\lvert x'(t)\rvert\le\bigl(\lvert\omega
     B-\gamma A\rvert+\lvert\gamma B+\omega A\rvert\bigr)e^{-\gamma t}$;
   and there are constants $C_{1},C_{2}>0$, depending only on $(m,k,c)$, with
   $$\lvert x(t)\rvert\le C_{1}r_{0},\qquad\lvert x'(t)\rvert\le C_{2}r_{0} \qquad(t\ge0),$$
   for the numerical SI coordinate values; equivalently the corresponding
   physical position and velocity are bounded by $(1\,\mathrm m)C_{1}r_{0}$
   and $(1\,\mathrm{m/s})C_{2}r_{0}$. Here $C_{1},C_{2}>0$ are dimensionless
   constants in the normalized SI coordinates and depend only on the
   numerical values of $(m,k,c)$ in the units declared by
   [[def-cm01-units]].
2. **Convergence.** For every maximal motion, $x(t)\to0$ and $x'(t)\to0$ as
   $t\to+\infty$ ([[def-limits-at-infinity]]).
3. **Asymptotic stability.** The rest point $(0,0)$ is Lyapunov stable and
   globally asymptotically stable in the sense of
   [[def-cm-equilibrium-and-lyapunov-stability]] for the model's phase
   system: for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that every
   maximal motion with $\lVert(x(t_{0}),x'(t_{0}))\rVert_{2}<\delta$ for some
   $t_{0}$ is defined for all $t\ge t_{0}$ and satisfies
   $\lVert(x(t),x'(t))\rVert_{2}<\varepsilon$ for all $t\ge t_{0}$; and
   every maximal motion satisfies $\lVert(x(t),x'(t))\rVert_{2}\to0$ as
   $t\to+\infty$. The norm is the Euclidean norm on the normalized numerical
   SI coordinates of [[def-cm04-phase-plane-and-energy-level-sets]].

The constants are explicit in the proof and no value of $m,k,c$ is asserted.

Adopt the damped oscillator model of [[post-cm04-linear-damping-model]] with
$m>0$, $k>0$, $c\ge0$, force law $F(x,v)=-kx-cv$ and mechanical energy
$E(x,v)=\tfrac12mv^{2}+\tfrac12kx^{2}$. Write
$$\Delta:=c^{2}-4mk,\qquad \gamma:=\frac{c}{2m},\qquad \lambda_{\pm}:=\frac{-c\pm\sqrt{\Delta}}{2m}\ (\Delta\ge0),\qquad \omega:=\frac{\sqrt{4mk-c^{2}}}{2m}\ (\Delta<0),$$
and note that $\Delta=-4mk<0$ and $\omega=\sqrt{k/m}$ when $c=0$. Then:

1. **Classification and uniqueness.** Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an
   interval with nonempty interior. A curve $x:J\to\mathbb R$ is a motion of
   the model if and only if it is one of the following:
   - $\Delta>0$: $x(t)=Ae^{\lambda_{+}t}+Be^{\lambda_{-}t}$ for reals $A,B$;
   - $\Delta=0$: $x(t)=(A+Bt)e^{-ct/(2m)}$ for reals $A,B$;
   - $\Delta<0$: $x(t)=e^{-\gamma t}\bigl(A\cos(\omega t)+B\sin(\omega
     t)\bigr)$ for reals $A,B$.
   For every datum $(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})$ there is exactly one maximal motion,
   it is defined on all of $\mathbb R$, and every motion with that datum is
   its restriction; when its family is written in $s=t-t_0$ instead of $t$, the coefficients
   are those supplied by clause 4 of
   [[thm-cm-homogeneous-oscillator-solution-classification]] for the shifted
   curve $s\mapsto x(t_{0}+s)$.
   In particular, for $c=0$ the motions are exactly those of the harmonic
   model of [[post-cm04-harmonic-model]] with the same $m$ and $k$.
2. **Energy dissipation.** For every motion $x:J\to\mathbb R$ the energy
   $e(t):=E(x(t),x'(t))$ is differentiable at every interior point of $J$
   with
   $$e'(t)=-c\,x'(t)^{2}\le0,$$
   and for $t_{1}<t_{2}$ in $J$ one has
   $e(t_{2})-e(t_{1})=-c\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}x'(s)^{2}\,ds\le0$: the energy is
   nonincreasing on $J$. If $c>0$, then the following are equivalent: (i)
   $e$ is constant on $J$; (ii) $x'(t)=0$ at every interior point of $J$;
   (iii) $x$ is constant on $J$; (iv) $x\equiv0$ on $J$, the rest motion of
   the model. Moreover, at every interior point with $x'(t)\neq0$ one has
   $e'(t)<0$, so the energy strictly decreases there.
3. **Rest points.** The rest points of the model are exactly the pairs
   $(x,0)$ with $kx=0$, that is $(0,0)$, and the constant curve $x\equiv0$ is
   its maximal motion with datum $(t_{0},0,0)$.

The statement is read for the declared data; it asserts no value of $m,k,c$
and no empirical decay law.

Adopt the harmonic model of [[post-cm04-harmonic-model]]: the
one-dimensional model of [[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]]
with $m>0$, $k>0$, force law $F(x)=-kx$ and potential $U(x)=\tfrac12kx^{2}$.
Write
$$\omega:=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}>0$$
for its **undamped frequency** in the sense of
[[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]]. Then:

1. **Motions.** Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty
   interior and let $t_{0}\in J$. A curve $x:J\to\mathbb R$ is a motion of the
   model on $J$ if and only if there are reals $A,B$ with
   $$x(t)=A\cos\bigl(\omega(t-t_{0})\bigr)+B\sin\bigl(\omega(t-t_{0})\bigr) \qquad(t\in J).$$
   For every datum $(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})$ there is exactly one maximal motion,
   it is defined on all of $\mathbb R$, and its coefficients are
   $A=x_{0}$, $B=v_{0}/\omega$; every motion with that datum is its
   restriction.
All claims involving every real time, periods or the whole phase ellipse below refer to the unique maximal extension of clause 1; on a local motion interval the same formulas hold by restriction.

2. **Amplitude and phase.** With $A,B$ as in clause 1 put
   $R:=\sqrt{A^{2}+B^{2}}$. Then $\lvert x(t)\rvert\le R$ for every $t$; if
   $R>0$ there is a real $\varphi$ with $\cos\varphi=A/R$ and
   $\sin\varphi=B/R$, and then
   $$x(t)=R\cos\bigl(\omega(t-t_{0})-\varphi\bigr)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R).$$
   If $R=0$ the motion is the rest motion $x\equiv0$.
3. **Period and frequency.** For every motion $x(t+T)=x(t)$ holds for all
   $t$ whenever $\omega T\in2\pi\mathbb Z$. If $R>0$, conversely every
   period $T>0$ of $x$ satisfies $\omega T\in2\pi\mathbb Z$, so the **least
   positive period** of the motion is $T_{\mathrm{per}}=2\pi/\omega$, and the
   **frequency** in cycles per second is $f=1/T_{\mathrm{per}}=\omega/(2\pi)$.
   If $R=0$ every $T$ is a period.
4. **Energy and phase curves.** Along every motion with coefficients $A,B$
   the mechanical energy is
   $$E\bigl(x(t),x'(t)\bigr)=\tfrac12k\bigl(A^{2}+B^{2}\bigr)=\tfrac12kR^{2}$$
   for every $t$, the phase curve is contained in the ellipse
   $$\Sigma_{R}:=\Bigl\{(x,v)\in\mathbb R^{2}:\frac{x^{2}}{R^{2}}+\frac{v^{2}}{\omega^{2}R^{2}}=1\Bigr\}$$
   when $R>0$, and it is exactly that ellipse: every point of $\Sigma_{R}$
   lies on the phase curve of the motion and is attained at exactly the times
   $t=t_{0}+\bigl(\theta_{1}+\varphi+2\pi n\bigr)/\omega$, $n\in\mathbb Z$,
   for the appropriate $\theta_{1}$. For $R=0$ the phase curve is the single
   point $(0,0)$, which is also the level set of energy $0$.
5. **Rest point.** The origin $(0,0)$ is the only rest point of the model,
   and it is Lyapunov stable, by
   [[pthm-cm04-equilibrium-stability-at-a-strict-minimum]]; no asymptotic
   stability is asserted.

The statement uses the declared data $m,k$ only through $\omega$ and the
energy; no value of $m$ or $k$ is asserted, and no real oscillator is claimed
to obey the model.

Let $m>0$, $k>0$, $c>0$ and $f_0\ne0$. For $\Omega\ge0$ let

$$A(\Omega):=\frac{|f_0|}{\sqrt{(k-m\Omega^2)^2+c^2\Omega^2}}$$

be the amplitude about zero of the steady response of [[thm-cm-forced-oscillator-sinusoidal-response]] clause 1, and put

$$u_*:=\frac{k}{m}-\frac{c^2}{2m^2},\qquad \Omega_*:=\sqrt{u_*}\ \ \text{when }u_*>0 .$$

Then:

1. If $u_*>0$ (equivalently $c^2<2mk$), $A$ is strictly increasing on $[0,\Omega_*]$, strictly decreasing on $[\Omega_*,\infty)$, and its maximum on $[0,\infty)$ is attained at $\Omega_*$ and at no other point, with
$$A(\Omega_*)=\frac{2m|f_0|}{c\sqrt{4mk-c^2}} .$$
2. If $u_*\le0$ then $A$ is strictly decreasing on $[0,\infty)$ and its maximum on $[0,\infty)$ is attained at $\Omega=0$ and at no other point.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

derivations.claim: Clause 1. Assume $D\neq0$. By [L2] the function $x_{p}$ is a solution of the forced equation on $\mathbb R$, hence a motion of the model by [L1], with the displayed real form and amplitude $\lvert x_{p}(t)\rvert\le A(\Omega)$. Its periodicity: the real form is a constant linear combination of $\cos(\Omega\cdot)$ and $\sin(\Omega\cdot)$, and for every real $u$ one has $\cos(u+2\pi)=\cos u$ and $\sin(u+2\pi)=\sin u$ by [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]]; taking $u=\Omega t$ and $u=\Omega(t+2\pi/\Omega)$ gives $x_{p}(t+2\pi/\Omega)=x_{p}(t)$.

Clause 2. The forced model has $k>0\ge0$ and the continuous drive $f_{0}\cos(\Omega t)$ on $I=\mathbb R$, so [L3] gives exactly one solution on $\mathbb R$ for every datum; hence every maximal motion is defined on $\mathbb R$. Let $x$ be a motion on an interval $J$ with nonempty interior and let $x_{p}$ be the particular motion of clause 1 or the resonant motion of [L2]. The function $y:=x-x_{p}$ is of class $C^{2}$ on $J$ and $$m\,y''+c\,y'+k\,y=\bigl(m\,x''+cx'+kx\bigr)-\bigl(m\,x_{p}''+cx_{p}'+kx_{p}\bigr) =f_{0}\cos(\Omega t)-f_{0}\cos(\Omega t)=0$$ by the linearity of the differential expression ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]; the two equations hold on $J$). Hence $y$ is a motion of the homogeneous damped model on $J$, and for $c=0$ it is a harmonic motion by [L1]. This is clause 2.
Clause 3, amplitude shape. For $f_0\ne0$ use [L6] on the amplitude function $A$ of clause 1; for $f_0=0$, the strictly positive denominator for $c>0$ gives $A(\Omega)=0$ for every $\Omega$ directly.

Clause 3, transient and boundedness. Let $c>0$; then $D\neq0$ because $D=0$ would force $c\Omega=0$ and hence $\Omega=0$, contrary to $\Omega>0$. Let $x$ be a motion; by clause 2, $y=x-x_{p}$ is a strictly damped homogeneous motion, so by [L4] $y(t)\to0$ and $y'(t)\to0$, and $x_{p}$, $x_{p}'$ are bounded by clause 1 and [L7]; hence $x(t)\to x_{p}(t)$ in the sense $x(t)-x_{p}(t)\to0$ and $x'(t)-x_{p}'(t)\to0$, and $x$ is bounded on $[0,\infty)$. If $x$ has datum $(t_{0},x_{p}(t_{0}),x_{p}'(t_{0}))$, then $y$ is a homogeneous motion with $y(t_{0})=y'(t_{0})=0$; by the uniqueness of [L4] (with the datum $(t_{0},0,0)$) $y\equiv0$, so $x=x_{p}$.

Clause 4. Let $c=0$ and $\Omega\neq\omega_{0}$. Then $D=k-m\Omega^{2}=m(\omega_{0}^{2}-\Omega^{2})\neq0$, so $x_{p}$ is a motion with $\lvert x_{p}(t)\rvert\le A(\Omega)$ by clause 1. Let $x$ be a motion on an interval with nonempty interior; by clause 2, $y=x-x_{p}$ is a harmonic motion, so by [L5] there is $R_{y}\ge0$ with $\lvert y(t)\rvert\le R_{y}$ for all $t$; hence $\lvert x(t)\rvert\le A(\Omega)+R_{y}$ on the interval, and since clause 2 extends the motion to $\mathbb R$, the motion is bounded on $\mathbb R$.

Clause 5. Let $c=0$, $\Omega=\omega_{0}$ and $f_{0}\neq0$. By [L2] the function $x_{p}(t)=f_{0}t\sin(\omega_{0}t)/(2m\omega_{0})$ is a motion on $\mathbb R$ and is unbounded on $[0,\infty)$. Let $x$ be any motion; by clause 2, $y=x-x_{p}$ is a harmonic motion, bounded by some $R_{y}$ by [L5]. Choose $t_{k}\to+\infty$ with $\lvert x_{p}(t_{k})\rvert\to+\infty$; then $\lvert x(t_{k})\rvert\ge\lvert x_{p}(t_{k})\rvert-\lvert y(t_{k})\rvert\ge\lvert x_{p}(t_{k})\rvert-R_{y}\to+\infty$, so $x$ is unbounded on $[0,\infty)$ as well, although $\lvert f_{0}\cos(\omega_{0}t)\rvert\le \lvert f_{0}\rvert$ is bounded by [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]]. This is clause 5.

Clause 6. For $c>0$ the computation of step 2.1 gives $D\neq0$ for every $\Omega>0$, and clause 3 supplies the boundedness. For $c=0$, $D=0\iff k=m\Omega^{2}\iff\Omega=\omega_{0}$ since $\Omega>0$ and $\omega_{0}>0$; clauses 4 and 5 give boundedness away from $\Omega=\omega_{0}$ and unboundedness at it when $f_0\ne0$. If $f_0=0$ the equation is homogeneous, so the harmonic classification [L5] gives boundedness also at that frequency.
