citations.quote:
**(i) Setting.** Work in the one-dimensional model class of
[[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]] with time window
$I_{0}=\mathbb R$, configuration domain $Q=\mathbb R$, a fixed mass $m>0$
and a **spring constant** $k>0$ of dimension $\mu\tau^{-2}$, read in newtons
per metre ([[def-cm01-units]]). The **harmonic model** is the model whose
force law is the **linear restoring force**
$$F(x,v):=-k\,x .$$
Its equation of motion is $m\,x''=-k\,x$, equivalently $m\,x''+k\,x=0$; the
model is autonomous and velocity-independent, and its potential is
$$U(x):=\tfrac12 k\,x^{2},$$
of dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (joules), which presents the force law in
the sense of clause (d) of [[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]]:
$U$ is of class $C^{2}$ in that clause's sense, and
$-U'(x)=-k\,x=F(x)$ ([[lem-derivative-of-a-power]],
[[def-derivative]]). The harmonic model is therefore a **conservative**
model of the class, with the potential representative $U$ declared above and
no residual force.

**(ii) Regularity and framework status.** Let
$X:=x_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm m)$ and
$V:=v_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm{m/s})$ be the dimensionless numerical SI state
coordinates (the real state coordinates in the displayed force-map signature),
and let $K:=k_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm{N/m})$ be the numerical
spring constant. In this representation the numerical force map
$\widehat F:=F_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm N)$ is
$\widehat F(X,V)=-KX$, so
$\lvert\widehat F(X,V)-\widehat F(X',V')\rvert\le
K\,\lVert(X,V)-(X',V')\rVert_{2}$. It is therefore locally Lipschitz in the
state variable with global numerical-coordinate constant $K$, uniformly in
time ([[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]). The harmonic model is
thus an admissible model of the class of clause (a) of
[[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]], and the existence,
uniqueness and conservation statements of this page apply to it. It is
adopted as a restricted model class of the framework, at the same primitive
level as the force maps of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]]: the force law
is model input.

**(iii) Physical reading and regime.** The model idealizes a **restoring
force linear in the displacement**: an ideal spring, or the quadratic
approximation of a potential $U$ near a strict local minimum $x_{*}$ with $U''(x_*)>0$, where
the Taylor expansion of the effective potential begins with the quadratic
term $\tfrac12 U''(x_{*})(x-x_{*})^{2}$ and the linearized equation carries
the **effective spring constant** $U''(x_{*})$ (the sources' linearization
procedure). The model is adopted for a stated regime — displacements so
small that the neglected remainder of the potential is adequate for the
purpose at hand — and it is **not** claimed to describe large-amplitude
oscillations, nonlinear springs, plasticity, or any given real system. The
coefficient $k$ is a model parameter, not a constant of the framework; when
its value is taken from a calibration experiment, that value is an empirical
premise carrying the apparatus conditions and the measurement uncertainty,
and the framework asserts none of it here. The linear form is the simplest
restoring law satisfying the standing regularity; that is a modelling
convenience, not a derivation.

**(iv) Status.** Adopted assumption of the framework when a model invokes
it; it selects no law of nature on its own. Every consequence below is a
conditional statement about the declared equation of motion.

Adopt the harmonic model of [[post-cm04-harmonic-model]]: the
one-dimensional model of [[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]]
with $m>0$, $k>0$, force law $F(x)=-kx$ and potential $U(x)=\tfrac12kx^{2}$.
Write
$$\omega:=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}>0$$
for its **undamped frequency** in the sense of
[[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]]. Then:

1. **Motions.** Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty
   interior and let $t_{0}\in J$. A curve $x:J\to\mathbb R$ is a motion of the
   model on $J$ if and only if there are reals $A,B$ with
   $$x(t)=A\cos\bigl(\omega(t-t_{0})\bigr)+B\sin\bigl(\omega(t-t_{0})\bigr) \qquad(t\in J).$$
   For every datum $(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})$ there is exactly one maximal motion,
   it is defined on all of $\mathbb R$, and its coefficients are
   $A=x_{0}$, $B=v_{0}/\omega$; every motion with that datum is its
   restriction.
All claims involving every real time, periods or the whole phase ellipse below refer to the unique maximal extension of clause 1; on a local motion interval the same formulas hold by restriction.

2. **Amplitude and phase.** With $A,B$ as in clause 1 put
   $R:=\sqrt{A^{2}+B^{2}}$. Then $\lvert x(t)\rvert\le R$ for every $t$; if
   $R>0$ there is a real $\varphi$ with $\cos\varphi=A/R$ and
   $\sin\varphi=B/R$, and then
   $$x(t)=R\cos\bigl(\omega(t-t_{0})-\varphi\bigr)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R).$$
   If $R=0$ the motion is the rest motion $x\equiv0$.
3. **Period and frequency.** For every motion $x(t+T)=x(t)$ holds for all
   $t$ whenever $\omega T\in2\pi\mathbb Z$. If $R>0$, conversely every
   period $T>0$ of $x$ satisfies $\omega T\in2\pi\mathbb Z$, so the **least
   positive period** of the motion is $T_{\mathrm{per}}=2\pi/\omega$, and the
   **frequency** in cycles per second is $f=1/T_{\mathrm{per}}=\omega/(2\pi)$.
   If $R=0$ every $T$ is a period.
4. **Energy and phase curves.** Along every motion with coefficients $A,B$
   the mechanical energy is
   $$E\bigl(x(t),x'(t)\bigr)=\tfrac12k\bigl(A^{2}+B^{2}\bigr)=\tfrac12kR^{2}$$
   for every $t$, the phase curve is contained in the ellipse
   $$\Sigma_{R}:=\Bigl\{(x,v)\in\mathbb R^{2}:\frac{x^{2}}{R^{2}}+\frac{v^{2}}{\omega^{2}R^{2}}=1\Bigr\}$$
   when $R>0$, and it is exactly that ellipse: every point of $\Sigma_{R}$
   lies on the phase curve of the motion and is attained at exactly the times
   $t=t_{0}+\bigl(\theta_{1}+\varphi+2\pi n\bigr)/\omega$, $n\in\mathbb Z$,
   for the appropriate $\theta_{1}$. For $R=0$ the phase curve is the single
   point $(0,0)$, which is also the level set of energy $0$.
5. **Rest point.** The origin $(0,0)$ is the only rest point of the model,
   and it is Lyapunov stable, by
   [[pthm-cm04-equilibrium-stability-at-a-strict-minimum]]; no asymptotic
   stability is asserted.

The statement uses the declared data $m,k$ only through $\omega$ and the
energy; no value of $m$ or $k$ is asserted, and no real oscillator is claimed
to obey the model.

Adopt a **conservative one-dimensional model**: the class of clause (a) of
[[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]] with a **time- and
velocity-independent** force law presented through a potential, that is
$$F(x)=-U'(x)\qquad(x\in Q)$$
for a function $U:Q\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^{2}$ (so the residual force of
clause (d) of that definition vanishes identically and the model is a global
potential model). Write
$$E(x,v)=\tfrac12 m v^{2}+U(x)$$
for the energy function of [[def-cm04-phase-plane-and-energy-level-sets]]
clause (b). Then:

1. **Existence and uniqueness.** Every datum $(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})$ with
   $t_{0}\in I_{0}$, $x_{0}\in Q$, $v_{0}\in\mathbb R$ has exactly one
   **maximal motion**: a motion $x:J_{\max}\to Q$ with $x(t_{0})=x_{0}$ and
   $x'(t_{0})=v_{0}$ that has no extension to a motion on a strictly larger
   interval. Its interval $J_{\max}$ is open, contains $t_{0}$ and is
   contained in $I_{0}$, and every motion of the model with the same datum is
   the restriction of $x$ to a subinterval.
2. **Energy conservation.** For every motion $x:J\to Q$ the function
   $t\mapsto E(x(t),x'(t))$ is constant on $J$.
3. **Level-set containment and velocity determination.** Let $x:J\to Q$ be
   a motion with datum $(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})$ and let $E_{0}:=E(x_{0},v_{0})$.
   Then $U(x(t))\le E_{0}$ for every $t\in J$; if $U(x(t))<E_{0}$ then
   $$x'(t)=\pm\sqrt{\frac{2\bigl(E_{0}-U(x(t))\bigr)}{m}},$$
   the two signs giving the only two possible values; and $x'(t)=0$ holds
   exactly when $U(x(t))=E_{0}$. In particular the phase curve of $x$ is
   contained in the energy level set $\Sigma_{E_{0}}$ of clause (b) of
   [[def-cm04-phase-plane-and-energy-level-sets]].
4. **Rest motions.** A point $x_{*}\in Q$ is an equilibrium of the model if
   and only if $U'(x_{*})=0$; in that case the constant curve
   $x\equiv x_{*}$ is the maximal motion with datum $(t_{0},x_{*},0)$, and
   conversely the maximal motion with datum $(t_{0},x_{*},0)$ is constant
   exactly when $U'(x_{*})=0$.

The statement is conditional on the declared potential $U$: replacing $U$ by
$U+c$ with a constant $c$ changes $E$ on the whole phase plane by $c$ and
leaves clauses 1, 3 and 4 unchanged. No claim of periodicity, boundedness of
the position or of the velocity, or approach to an equilibrium is made.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

For every real $x$,
$$\sin x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=m\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z,\qquad \cos x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=(m+1/2)\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z.$$
Both sine and cosine have period $2\pi$, and no smaller positive number is a common period.

**(a) Dimensions.** Write $\ell$, $\tau$, $\mu$ for the three independent *dimension symbols* of length, duration and mass. A **dimension** is an element of the free abelian group generated by $\ell,\tau,\mu$, that is, a triple $(a,b,c)\in\mathbb Z^3$ written $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}$; **products and inverses** of dimensions are componentwise addition and negation, so that $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}\cdot\ell^{a'}\tau^{b'}\mu^{c'}=\ell^{a+a'}\tau^{b+b'}\mu^{c+c'}$ and $(\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c})^{-1}=\ell^{-a}\tau^{-b}\mu^{-c}$. The **dimensionless** dimension is $\ell^{0}\tau^{0}\mu^{0}$, abbreviated $1$.

**(b) The dimension map.** The conventions assign to the quantities of the framework a **dimension** $[X]$, subject to the rules

$$[XY]=[X][Y],\qquad [X/Y]=[X][Y]^{-1},\qquad \left[\frac{dX}{du}\right]=[X][u]^{-1},$$

and to the requirement that a sum $X+Y$ is meaningful only when $[X]=[Y]$, in which case $[X+Y]=[X]$. The third rule applies to a differentiable dependence of a quantity $X$ on a quantity $u$ and covers iterated differentiation, so that $[d^{2}X/du^{2}]=[X][u]^{-2}$. The assignment is part of the conventions: the rules above are consistency requirements on it, not physical laws and not theorems.

**(c) Reference units.** The **metre** is the reference unit of length, the **second** the reference unit of duration and the **kilogram** the reference unit of mass. A quantity of dimension $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}$ is expressed in the unit $\mathrm m^{a}\,\mathrm s^{b}\,\mathrm{kg}^{c}$: its value is a real multiple of that unit, and the conventions fix how the numerical value of a quantity is read (a coordinate value alone is a real number, and the unit declaration attaches its dimension). The coordinates of an adapted chart of [[def-cm-affine-time-space]] are read with the time coordinate $t$ in seconds, $[t]=\tau$, and the spatial coordinate components $x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}$ in metres, $[x_{i}]=\ell$; the slice distance $d_{g}$ of [[def-cm-affine-time-space]] between simultaneous events is read in metres.

**(d) Typed quantity conventions.** The following constructions specify the quantities whose dimensions are recorded here, without adopting their dynamics. Fix a positive integer $N$, a nondegenerate open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ with time parameter $t$ in seconds, position curves $x_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^2$ with components in metres, and constant parameters $m_i>0$ in kilograms, for $1\le i\le N$. Derivatives and integrals have the meanings of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]. These are conditional numerical constructions in a fixed spatial coordinate system; whether they represent a particular system is a separate model assumption.

1. **Velocity and acceleration** are the maps $w_i=x_i':I\to\mathbb R^3$ and $a_i=x_i'':I\to\mathbb R^3$, of dimensions $\ell\tau^{-1}$ and $\ell\tau^{-2}$ componentwise.
2. The **mass operator** is the linear map $\mathsf M:(\mathbb R^3)^N\to(\mathbb R^3)^N$, $\mathsf M(z_1,\ldots,z_N)=(m_1z_1,\ldots,m_Nz_N)$, with dimension $\mu$; the **momentum** of label $i$ is $p_i=m_iw_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$, with component dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$.
3. A **force input** is a specified map $F:I\times O\times\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N}$, where $O\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ is open, its arguments are time, positions and velocities, and each output component has dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$. No regularity or equation equating $F$ with $\mathsf M x''$ is adopted here. A later model must state both if needed.
4. For a specified scalar **potential energy** map $U:I\times O\to\mathbb R$ of dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-2}$ and a tuple $x(t)\in O$, the **kinetic energy** is $T(t)=\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^N m_i\sum_{j=1}^3(w_i(t))_j^2$, and the **mechanical energy** is $E(t)=T(t)+U(t,x(t))$. Both are real-valued and have dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-2}$; no conservation or applicability to every interaction is asserted.
5. Given a scalar map $L:I\times O\times\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R$ of the energy dimension and $t_0<t_1$ in $I$, assume $t\mapsto L(t,x(t),w(t))$ is integrable on $[t_0,t_1]$. Its **action on this curve segment** is the real number $S[x;t_0,t_1]=\int_{t_0}^{t_1}L(t,x(t),w(t))\,dt$, with dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-1}$ (the integration convention multiplies the integrand's dimension by duration). No variational principle is imposed.
6. Relative to the chosen spatial origin, define the **angular momentum** $J_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ by $J_i(t)=x_i(t)\times p_i(t)$, where for $r,s\in\mathbb R^3$ the operation is explicitly $r\times s=(r_2s_3-r_3s_2,r_3s_1-r_1s_3,r_1s_2-r_2s_1)$. Its components have dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-1}$. These quantities depend on the chosen coordinates; dimensions alone assert no transformation or conservation law.
7. A **rotation matrix** here means a real $3\times3$ matrix $R$ satisfying $R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3$ and $\det R=1$; its entries are dimensionless. A radian angle is an arc length divided by its positive radius, hence dimensionless. A generalized coordinate means a component of a specified local coordinate chart on a configuration space; each such component has its own declared dimension, and only quantities of equal dimension are added.

**(e) Conventions only.** No numerical value of any constant or parameter of a model is fixed by this item: in particular no mass, length or duration of any concrete system is asserted, and no measured value is recorded. Two numerical values that are equal but carry different dimensions are not thereby the same quantity. Where a treatment or a later item suppresses a dimensionful constant by a natural-unit convention, that convention is read as shorthand for the corresponding SI-dimensioned statement with the constant restored, and it changes no dimension fixed here.

derivations.claim: The frequency is $\omega=\sqrt{k/m}=\sqrt{4}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}=2\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$ by [L1] and [L3], and $A=x_{0}=0$, $B=v_{0}/\omega=\tfrac12$ m. By clause 1 of [[pthm-cm04-harmonic-motion]] the curve $x(t)=\tfrac12\sin(2t)$ is the unique maximal motion with the declared datum, defined on $\mathbb R$.

Amplitude and phase: $R=\sqrt{0^{2}+(1/2)^{2}}=\tfrac12$ m; taking $\varphi=\pi/2$ gives $\cos\varphi=0=A/R$ and $\sin\varphi=1=B/R$ by [L2], so clause 2 of [[pthm-cm04-harmonic-motion]] gives $x(t)=\tfrac12\cos(2t-\pi/2)=\tfrac12\sin(2t)$, the displayed curve.

Period and frequency: $R>0$, so by clause 3 of [[pthm-cm04-harmonic-motion]] the least positive period is $2\pi/\omega=\pi$ s, and the frequency is $1/\pi$ cycles per second; indeed $\sin(2(t+\pi))=\sin(2t+2\pi)=\sin(2t)$ by [L2].

Energy: by clause 4 of [[pthm-cm04-harmonic-motion]], $E=\tfrac12kR^{2}=\tfrac12\cdot4\cdot\tfrac14=\tfrac12$ J, constant in $t$. Directly, with $x'(t)=\cos(2t)$ by [L2], $$E(x(t),x'(t))=\tfrac12\cos^{2}(2t)+2\cdot\tfrac14\sin^{2}(2t) =\tfrac12\bigl(\cos^{2}(2t)+\sin^{2}(2t)\bigr)=\tfrac12,$$ using [L1] and the Pythagorean identity of [L2].

Phase ellipse: with $R^{2}=\tfrac14$ and $\omega^{2}R^{2}=1$, the ellipse of clause 4 is $4x^{2}+v^{2}=1$; the phase curve $\bigl(\tfrac12\sin(2t),\cos(2t)\bigr)$ satisfies $4\cdot\tfrac14\sin^{2}(2t)+\cos^{2}(2t)=1$ by [L2], and by clause 4 of [[pthm-cm04-harmonic-motion]] it fills the ellipse; the amplitude $\tfrac12$ m is attained at $t=\pi/4+n\pi/2$, $n\in\mathbb Z$, where $\cos(2t-\pi/2)=\pm1$.

boundaries.reason: The check declares one model and one datum; no possibly empty family is quantified.

boundaries.evidence: The zero-displacement initial datum x_0=0 is the declared data; the phase choice cos(phi)=0, sin(phi)=1 at step 2.1 is the zero-cosine case, and the equilibrium case R=0 is not the declared datum.
The model is one-dimensional and the check evaluates a single motion; the period and energy identities at steps 2.2-2.3 are scalar.

boundaries.reason: The declared data have R=1/2>0, so no degenerate amplitude or zero-energy level occurs in this check; the general degenerate case belongs to the item theorem.

boundaries.evidence: The base time t_0=0 lies in R and the least period pi is evaluated over all t; the amplitude times t=pi/4+n pi/2 of step 3.1 are interior points of R.

boundaries.reason: All quantities are computed from the declared data; no selection is made.
The check verifies the theorem clauses constructively and is not an equivalence statement.
The Example verifies the particular sine motion, least period, energy and phase ellipse at the fixed datum; it is not a characterization of arbitrary phase-plane curves.

citations.quote:
Adopt the damped oscillator model of [[post-cm04-linear-damping-model]] with
$m>0$, $k>0$, $c\ge0$, force law $F(x,v)=-kx-cv$ and mechanical energy
$E(x,v)=\tfrac12mv^{2}+\tfrac12kx^{2}$. Write
$$\Delta:=c^{2}-4mk,\qquad \gamma:=\frac{c}{2m},\qquad \lambda_{\pm}:=\frac{-c\pm\sqrt{\Delta}}{2m}\ (\Delta\ge0),\qquad \omega:=\frac{\sqrt{4mk-c^{2}}}{2m}\ (\Delta<0),$$
and note that $\Delta=-4mk<0$ and $\omega=\sqrt{k/m}$ when $c=0$. Then:

1. **Classification and uniqueness.** Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an
   interval with nonempty interior. A curve $x:J\to\mathbb R$ is a motion of
   the model if and only if it is one of the following:
   - $\Delta>0$: $x(t)=Ae^{\lambda_{+}t}+Be^{\lambda_{-}t}$ for reals $A,B$;
   - $\Delta=0$: $x(t)=(A+Bt)e^{-ct/(2m)}$ for reals $A,B$;
   - $\Delta<0$: $x(t)=e^{-\gamma t}\bigl(A\cos(\omega t)+B\sin(\omega
     t)\bigr)$ for reals $A,B$.
   For every datum $(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})$ there is exactly one maximal motion,
   it is defined on all of $\mathbb R$, and every motion with that datum is
   its restriction; when its family is written in $s=t-t_0$ instead of $t$, the coefficients
   are those supplied by clause 4 of
   [[thm-cm-homogeneous-oscillator-solution-classification]] for the shifted
   curve $s\mapsto x(t_{0}+s)$.
   In particular, for $c=0$ the motions are exactly those of the harmonic
   model of [[post-cm04-harmonic-model]] with the same $m$ and $k$.
2. **Energy dissipation.** For every motion $x:J\to\mathbb R$ the energy
   $e(t):=E(x(t),x'(t))$ is differentiable at every interior point of $J$
   with
   $$e'(t)=-c\,x'(t)^{2}\le0,$$
   and for $t_{1}<t_{2}$ in $J$ one has
   $e(t_{2})-e(t_{1})=-c\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}x'(s)^{2}\,ds\le0$: the energy is
   nonincreasing on $J$. If $c>0$, then the following are equivalent: (i)
   $e$ is constant on $J$; (ii) $x'(t)=0$ at every interior point of $J$;
   (iii) $x$ is constant on $J$; (iv) $x\equiv0$ on $J$, the rest motion of
   the model. Moreover, at every interior point with $x'(t)\neq0$ one has
   $e'(t)<0$, so the energy strictly decreases there.
3. **Rest points.** The rest points of the model are exactly the pairs
   $(x,0)$ with $kx=0$, that is $(0,0)$, and the constant curve $x\equiv0$ is
   its maximal motion with datum $(t_{0},0,0)$.

The statement is read for the declared data; it asserts no value of $m,k,c$
and no empirical decay law.

Let $m>0$, $c\ge0$ and $k>0$, and consider the homogeneous damped oscillator model $m\,x''+c\,x'+k\,x=0$ of [[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]] with time domain $I=\mathbb R$ and forcing $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ identically zero, with characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda)=m\lambda^2+c\lambda+k$, discriminant $\Delta=c^2-4mk$, damping rate $\gamma:=c/(2m)$, and, when applicable, roots
$$\lambda_\pm:=\frac{-c\pm\sqrt\Delta}{2m}\ (\Delta\ge0),\qquad \lambda:=-\frac{c}{2m},\qquad \omega:=\frac{\sqrt{4mk-c^2}}{2m}\ (\Delta<0).$$

A local solution here may have any interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ with nonempty interior, with domain-relative derivatives at included endpoints. It has a unique extension to the global family below. A **maximal solution** means one that has no solution extension to a strictly larger interval; the maximal solutions of this global autonomous equation are precisely the family members on $\mathbb R$. For a homogeneous model restricted to a time domain $I$, its solutions have $J\subseteq I$ and are restrictions of these same global members; their extensions solve the all-$\mathbb R$ equation.

1. **Distinct real roots.** If $\Delta>0$, then $\lambda_+>\lambda_-$ are exactly the real roots of $p$, and a function $x:J\to\mathbb R$ on an interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ with nonempty interior is a solution of the model if and only if
$$x(t)=Ae^{\lambda_+t}+Be^{\lambda_-t}\quad(t\in J)$$
for some $A,B\in\mathbb R$.

2. **Double real root.** If $\Delta=0$, then $\lambda=-c/(2m)$ is the only root of $p$, and $x:J\to\mathbb R$ is a solution if and only if
$$x(t)=(A+Bt)e^{\lambda t}\quad(t\in J)$$
for some $A,B\in\mathbb R$.

3. **Complex conjugate roots.** If $\Delta<0$, then $\omega>0$, the roots of $p$ are $-\gamma\pm i\omega$, and $x:J\to\mathbb R$ is a solution if and only if
$$x(t)=e^{-\gamma t}\bigl(A\cos(\omega t)+B\sin(\omega t)\bigr)\quad(t\in J)$$
for some $A,B\in\mathbb R$.

4. **Initial data.** In each of the three cases and for every $(x_0,v_0)\in\mathbb R^2$ there is exactly one solution $x:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ with $x(0)=x_0$ and $x'(0)=v_0$. Its coefficients are
$$A=\frac{v_0-\lambda_-x_0}{\lambda_+-\lambda_-},\quad B=\frac{\lambda_+x_0-v_0}{\lambda_+-\lambda_-}\quad(\Delta>0),\qquad A=x_0,\ B=v_0-\lambda x_0\quad(\Delta=0),$$
$$A=x_0,\quad B=\frac{v_0+\gamma x_0}{\omega}\quad(\Delta<0).$$

Adopt the damped oscillator model of [[post-cm04-linear-damping-model]] with
$m>0$, $k>0$ and $c>0$ (strict damping), force law $F(x,v)=-kx-cv$ and
energy $E(x,v)=\tfrac12mv^{2}+\tfrac12kx^{2}$. Position and velocity
coordinates in every phase norm below are their normalized numerical SI
values, as defined in clause (a) of
[[def-cm04-phase-plane-and-energy-level-sets]]. For the datum
$(0,x_{0},v_{0})$, put $r_{0}:=\lVert(x_{0},v_{0})\rVert_{2}$ in that norm.
In displayed time-dependent formulas, $t$ is read numerically in seconds,
and rates in exponents are read in inverse seconds. Write
$\Delta=c^{2}-4mk$, $\gamma=c/(2m)>0$,
$\lambda_{\pm}=(-c\pm\sqrt{\Delta})/(2m)$ for $\Delta\ge0$,
$\lambda=-c/(2m)$ for $\Delta=0$ and $\omega=\sqrt{4mk-c^{2}}/(2m)$ for
$\Delta<0$. Then:

1. **Motion bounds.** For every motion $x:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ of the model
   with datum $(0,x_{0},v_{0})$ and phase norm $r_{0}$ the following bounds
   hold for all $t\ge0$, with the coefficients $A,B$ of the
   classification of [[pthm-cm04-damped-motion]]:
   - $\Delta>0$: $\lvert x(t)\rvert\le(\lvert A\rvert+\lvert
     B\rvert)e^{\lambda_{+}t}$ and
     $\lvert x'(t)\rvert\le\bigl(\lvert\lambda_{+}\rvert\lvert
     A\rvert+\lvert\lambda_{-}\rvert\lvert B\rvert\bigr)e^{\lambda_{+}t}$;
   - $\Delta=0$: $\lvert x(t)\rvert\le(\lvert A\rvert+\lvert
     B\rvert t)e^{\lambda t}$ and
     $\lvert x'(t)\rvert\le\bigl(\lvert\lambda A+B\rvert+\lvert\lambda
     B\rvert t\bigr)e^{\lambda t}$;
   - $\Delta<0$: $\lvert x(t)\rvert\le(\lvert A\rvert+\lvert
     B\rvert)e^{-\gamma t}$ and $\lvert x'(t)\rvert\le\bigl(\lvert\omega
     B-\gamma A\rvert+\lvert\gamma B+\omega A\rvert\bigr)e^{-\gamma t}$;
   and there are constants $C_{1},C_{2}>0$, depending only on $(m,k,c)$, with
   $$\lvert x(t)\rvert\le C_{1}r_{0},\qquad\lvert x'(t)\rvert\le C_{2}r_{0} \qquad(t\ge0),$$
   for the numerical SI coordinate values; equivalently the corresponding
   physical position and velocity are bounded by $(1\,\mathrm m)C_{1}r_{0}$
   and $(1\,\mathrm{m/s})C_{2}r_{0}$. Here $C_{1},C_{2}>0$ are dimensionless
   constants in the normalized SI coordinates and depend only on the
   numerical values of $(m,k,c)$ in the units declared by
   [[def-cm01-units]].
2. **Convergence.** For every maximal motion, $x(t)\to0$ and $x'(t)\to0$ as
   $t\to+\infty$ ([[def-limits-at-infinity]]).
3. **Asymptotic stability.** The rest point $(0,0)$ is Lyapunov stable and
   globally asymptotically stable in the sense of
   [[def-cm-equilibrium-and-lyapunov-stability]] for the model's phase
   system: for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that every
   maximal motion with $\lVert(x(t_{0}),x'(t_{0}))\rVert_{2}<\delta$ for some
   $t_{0}$ is defined for all $t\ge t_{0}$ and satisfies
   $\lVert(x(t),x'(t))\rVert_{2}<\varepsilon$ for all $t\ge t_{0}$; and
   every maximal motion satisfies $\lVert(x(t),x'(t))\rVert_{2}\to0$ as
   $t\to+\infty$. The norm is the Euclidean norm on the normalized numerical
   SI coordinates of [[def-cm04-phase-plane-and-energy-level-sets]].

The constants are explicit in the proof and no value of $m,k,c$ is asserted.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

Throughout, $+\infty$ and $-\infty$ are **abbreviations and not real numbers**,
exactly as in [[def-interval]] and [[def-divergence-to-infinity]]. Every phrase
below is a single abbreviation for a displayed condition on reals, and no
arithmetic is ever performed with the symbols.

**Limits at $+\infty$.** Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be **not bounded above**
([[def-bounded-set]]), let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$. We
write

$$\lim_{x \to +\infty} f(x) = L$$

when for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real $M$ such that

$$|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon \qquad \text{for every } x \in A \text{ with } x > M .$$

**Limits at $-\infty$.** Let $A$ be **not bounded below**. We write
$\lim_{x \to -\infty} f(x) = L$ when for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a
real $M$ with $|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon$ for every $x \in A$ with $x < M$.

**Why unboundedness is required.** It plays exactly the role the limit-point
condition plays in [[def-function-limit]]. Saying that $A$ is not bounded above
says that no real is an upper bound of $A$, that is, that for every real $M$
there is $x \in A$ with $x > M$ ([[def-bounded-set]],
[[def-complete-ordered-field]]); so the set over which the condition quantifies
is never empty and the condition is never vacuous. Without the hypothesis every
real $L$ would satisfy it and the notation would not denote.

**Uniqueness, proved here.** Suppose $A$ is not bounded above and
$\lim_{x \to +\infty} f(x) = L$ and $\lim_{x \to +\infty} f(x) = L'$ with
$L \ne L'$. Then $|L - L'| > 0$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]]), so
$\varepsilon := |L - L'|/2 > 0$ ([[cor-of-one-positive]],
[[lem-of-inverse-positive]], [[lem-of-sign-rules]]). Choose reals $M_1, M_2$
witnessing the two conditions at this $\varepsilon$ and let $M$ be the larger of
them, the order being total. Since $A$ is not bounded above there is $x \in A$
with $x > M$, hence with $x > M_1$ and $x > M_2$, and then

$$|L - L'| = |(L - f(x)) + (f(x) - L')| \le |f(x) - L| + |f(x) - L'| < 2\varepsilon = |L - L'|$$

([[lem-of-triangle-inequality]], [[lem-of-abs-value]], [[lem-of-add-order]]),
which trichotomy forbids. So $L = L'$, and the notation
$\lim_{x \to +\infty} f(x)$ denotes a single real. The same four lines, with the
inequalities on $x$ reversed, give uniqueness at $-\infty$.

**Infinite limits at a point.** Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c$ be a limit
point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) and let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$. We write

$$f(x) \to +\infty \ \text{ as } \ x \to c$$

when for every real $M$ there is a real $\delta > 0$ such that $f(x) > M$ for
every $x \in A$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$; and $f(x) \to -\infty$ as $x \to c$
when for every real $M$ there is a real $\delta > 0$ with $f(x) < M$ for every
such $x$.

**This library does not write $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = +\infty$.** The right-hand
side would not be an element of $\mathbb{R}$, and writing the equation would
silently move the discussion into the extended real line, a structure that is
not a field. That is the convention already fixed by
[[def-divergence-to-infinity]] for sequences and by [[rem-sup-conventions]] for

$$\exp(x)\to+\infty\quad(x\to+\infty),\qquad \exp(x)\to0\quad(x\to-\infty),$$

derivations.claim: Discriminants and coefficients. With $m=k=1$ and $x_{0}=1$, $v_{0}=0$ the three discriminants are $\Delta=1-4=-3$, $\Delta=4-4=0$ and $\Delta=25-4=21$. In the first case $\gamma=\tfrac12$, $\omega=\sqrt{4-1}/2=\sqrt3/2$, $A=1$ and $B=(0+\tfrac12)/(\sqrt3/2)=1/\sqrt3$. In the second $\lambda=-2/(2\cdot1)=-1$, $A=1$, $B=0-(-1)\cdot1=1$. In the third $\lambda_{\pm}=(-5\pm\sqrt{21})/2$, $\lambda_{+}-\lambda_{-}=\sqrt{21}$, $A=(0-\lambda_{-})/\sqrt{21}=(5+\sqrt{21})/(2\sqrt{21})$ and $B=(\lambda_{+}-0)/\sqrt{21}=(\sqrt{21}-5)/(2\sqrt{21})$. By [L1] the three displayed curves are the unique maximal motions with the datum in the three cases, and all are defined on $\mathbb R$.

Initial data. In the first case $x(0)=\cos0+(1/\sqrt3)\sin0=1$ and, by [L2], $$x'(t)=e^{-t/2}\Bigl[-\tfrac12\Bigl(\cos\tfrac{\sqrt3t}{2}+\tfrac1{\sqrt3}\sin\tfrac{\sqrt3t}{2}\Bigr) -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\sin\tfrac{\sqrt3t}{2}+\tfrac12\cos\tfrac{\sqrt3t}{2}\Bigr] =-\tfrac{2}{\sqrt3}\,e^{-t/2}\sin\tfrac{\sqrt3\,t}{2},$$ so $x'(0)=0$. In the second case $x(0)=1$ and $x'(t)=e^{-t}-(1+t)e^{-t}=-t\,e^{-t}$ by [L2], so $x'(0)=0$. In the third case $x(0)=A+B=\bigl(5+\sqrt{21}+\sqrt{21}-5\bigr)/(2\sqrt{21})=1$ and $x'(0)=\lambda_{+}A+\lambda_{-}B=\bigl[-(5-\sqrt{21})(5+\sqrt{21})-(5+\sqrt{21})(\sqrt{21}-5)\bigr]/(4\sqrt{21})=0$ since $\lambda_+ A=-1/\sqrt{21}$ and $\lambda_- B=1/\sqrt{21}$. Hence $x'(t)=(e^{\lambda_-t}-e^{\lambda_+t})/\sqrt{21}$; strict monotonicity of the exponential and $\lambda_-<\lambda_+$ show that this vanishes exactly at $t=0$.

Energy. With $m=k=1$ the energy is $E=\tfrac12v^{2}+\tfrac12x^{2}$, and $E(0)=\tfrac12\cdot0+\tfrac12\cdot1=\tfrac12$ J in all three cases. By [L1] the identity $E'(t)=-c\,x'(t)^{2}$ holds along each motion, so $E'(t)<0$ exactly when $x'(t)\ne0$. In the first case the exceptional times are $t=2\pi n/\sqrt3$ for every $n\in\mathbb Z$, by the sine zero set and the positive exponential factor in step 2.1. In the second and third cases the derivative vanishes only at $t=0$ and $E'(t)<0$ for every $t\ne0$. In particular no motion here is a constant-energy motion other than the rest motion, consistent with clause 2 of [[pthm-cm04-damped-motion]].

By clause 1 of [[pthm-cm04-damped-decay-and-stability]] the following bounds hold for $t\ge0$: in the first case $\lvert x(t)\rvert\le(1+1/\sqrt3)e^{-t/2}$, in the second $\lvert x(t)\rvert\le(1+t)e^{-t}$ and in the third $\lvert x(t)\rvert\le\frac{5}{\sqrt{21}}e^{(-5+\sqrt{21})t/2}$, because $\lvert A\rvert+\lvert B\rvert=(5+\sqrt{21}+5-\sqrt{21})/(2\sqrt{21})=5/\sqrt{21}$ as $\sqrt{21}<5$. Evaluated at $t=4$: the bounds are $(1+1/\sqrt3)e^{-2}\approx0.2135$, $5e^{-4}\approx0.0916$ and $\frac{5}{\sqrt{21}}e^{-10+2\sqrt{21}} \approx1.0911\cdot0.4339\approx0.4735$, while the explicit curves give $\lvert x(4)\rvert\approx0.1531$, $\lvert x(4)\rvert=5e^{-4}\approx0.0916$ and $\lvert x(4)\rvert\approx0.4537$. citations.quote:
Adopt the sinusoidally driven oscillator model of
[[post-cm04-sinusoidal-drive-model]] with data $m>0$, $k>0$, $c\ge0$,
$f_{0}\in\mathbb R$ and $\Omega>0$, force law
$F(t,x,v)=f_{0}\cos(\Omega t)-kx-cv$ and equation
$m\,x''+cx'+kx=f_{0}\cos(\Omega t)$. Put
$$\omega_{0}:=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}},\qquad D:=k-m\Omega^{2}+i\,c\,\Omega\in\mathbb C,$$
and define the **steady response**
$$x_{p}(t):=\operatorname{Re}\Bigl(\frac{f_{0}e^{i\Omega t}}{D}\Bigr) =\frac{f_{0}\bigl[(k-m\Omega^{2})\cos(\Omega t)+c\,\Omega\sin(\Omega t)\bigr]} {(k-m\Omega^{2})^{2}+c^{2}\Omega^{2}}\qquad(D\neq0),$$
with **amplitude** $A(\Omega):=\lvert f_{0}\rvert/\sqrt{(k-m\Omega^{2})^{2}+c^{2}\Omega^{2}}$,
and in the exceptional case $c=0$, $\Omega=\omega_{0}$ define
$x_{p}(t):=f_{0}t\sin(\omega_{0}t)/(2m\omega_{0})$. All all-time boundedness, convergence and unboundedness claims below refer to maximal motions on $\mathbb R$; local motions are their restrictions as in clause 2. Then:

1. **Steady response.** If $D\neq0$ — that is $c>0$, or $c=0$ and
   $\Omega\neq\omega_{0}$ — then $x_{p}$ is a motion of the model on
   $\mathbb R$, of period $2\pi/\Omega$, with amplitude $A(\Omega)$ in the
   sense $\lvert x_{p}(t)\rvert\le A(\Omega)$ for all $t$ and equality at
   suitable times.
2. **Reduction to the homogeneous model.** Every datum has exactly one
   maximal motion, it is defined on all of $\mathbb R$, and every motion
   $x$ of the model on an interval with nonempty interior can be written
   $x=x_{p}+y$, where $x_{p}$ is the particular motion of clause 1, or the
   resonant motion in the exceptional case, and $y$ is a motion of the damped
   homogeneous model with the same $m$, $c$, $k$ (and is a harmonic motion
   of [[post-cm04-harmonic-model]] when $c=0$).
3. **Strictly damped case $c>0$.** For every $\Omega>0$ the following hold:
  every motion is bounded on $[0,\infty)$; and
   $x(t)-x_{p}(t)\to0$ and $x'(t)-x_{p}'(t)\to0$ as $t\to+\infty$. Moreover
   $x_{p}$ is the unique motion with datum
   $(t_{0},x_{p}(t_{0}),x_{p}'(t_{0}))$ for any $t_{0}\in\mathbb R$. The
   amplitude function $\Omega\mapsto A(\Omega)$ has the following shape when $f_0\ne0$: if
   $c^{2}<2mk$ it is strictly increasing on $(0,\Omega_{*})$ and strictly
   decreasing on $(\Omega_{*},\infty)$, so has its unique maximum there, with
   $$\Omega_{*}=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}-\frac{c^{2}}{2m^{2}}},\qquad A(\Omega_{*})=\frac{2m\lvert f_{0}\rvert}{c\sqrt{4mk-c^{2}}};$$
   if $c^{2}\ge2mk$ it is strictly decreasing on $(0,\infty)$ and does not
   attain a maximum on the declared positive-frequency domain. Its continuous
   extension to $\Omega=0$ has its maximum there. For $f_0=0$ the amplitude is
   identically zero on the domain, so every frequency has the same value.
4. **Undamped case away from resonance.** For $c=0$ and
   $\Omega\neq\omega_{0}$ every motion is bounded on $\mathbb R$.
5. **Undamped resonance.** For $c=0$, $\Omega=\omega_{0}$ and $f_{0}\neq0$
   the motion $x_{p}(t)=f_{0}t\sin(\omega_{0}t)/(2m\omega_{0})$ is unbounded
   on $[0,\infty)$, and every motion of the model is unbounded on
   $[0,\infty)$, although the drive $t\mapsto f_{0}\cos(\omega_{0}t)$ is
   bounded.
6. **Off the singular cases.** For $c>0$ the denominator never vanishes and
   every $\Omega>0$ is admissible; for $c=0$ the exceptional frequency is
   exactly $\Omega=\omega_{0}$. Consequently the boundedness assertions of
   clauses 3 and 4 hold for $c>0$, and for $c=0$ away from $\Omega=\omega_{0}$,
   and also at undamped resonance when $f_0=0$; for a nonzero drive clause 5 gives unboundedness at undamped resonance.

The statement is read for the declared model data; no value of any parameter
and no measured response is asserted.

Let $m>0$, $k>0$, $c\ge0$, let $f_0\in\mathbb R$ and $\Omega\ge0$, and consider the forced model $m\,x''+c\,x'+k\,x=f$ with time domain $I=\mathbb R$ and forcing $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, $f(t)=f_0\cos(\Omega t)$ ([[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]]). Put

$$D:=k-m\Omega^2+i\,c\,\Omega\in\mathbb C,\qquad \omega_0:=\sqrt{k/m}.$$

1. **Non-resonant response.** If $D\ne0$, then the function
$$x_p(t):=\operatorname{Re}\!\left(\frac{f_0e^{i\Omega t}}{D}\right)=f_0\,\frac{(k-m\Omega^2)\cos(\Omega t)+c\,\Omega\sin(\Omega t)}{(k-m\Omega^2)^2+c^2\Omega^2}$$
is a solution of the forced model on all of $\mathbb R$. Its amplitude about zero is $|f_0|/\sqrt{(k-m\Omega^2)^2+c^2\Omega^2}$. For $\Omega>0$ and $f_0\ne0$, a **phase-lag angle relative to the drive** means a real $\phi$ such that $x_p(t)=(f_0/|D|)\cos(\Omega t-\phi)$ for every $t$, with the signed factor $f_0$ retained in both drive and response. Such an angle exists: any $\phi\in\mathbb R$ satisfying
$$\cos\phi=\frac{k-m\Omega^2}{|D|},\qquad\sin\phi=\frac{c\Omega}{|D|}$$
has this property. No temporal phase is assigned when $\Omega=0$ or $f_0=0$.

2. **Resonance.** If $c=0$ and $\Omega=\omega_0$, then $D=0$ and
$$x_p(t):=\frac{f_0\,t\sin(\omega_0t)}{2m\omega_0}$$
is a solution of the forced model on all of $\mathbb R$; if $f_0\ne0$ then $x_p$ is unbounded on $[0,\infty)$.

3. **Transient decay.** If $c>0$, then $D\ne0$ for every $\Omega\ge0$, and every solution $x:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ of the forced model satisfies
$$x(t)=x_p(t)+x_h(t)$$
where $x_h$ is a homogeneous solution; consequently $x(t)-x_p(t)\to0$ as $t\to+\infty$ ([[def-limits-at-infinity]]) and $x$ is bounded on $[0,\infty)$.

Let $m>0$, $k>0$, $c>0$ and $f_0\ne0$. For $\Omega\ge0$ let

$$A(\Omega):=\frac{|f_0|}{\sqrt{(k-m\Omega^2)^2+c^2\Omega^2}}$$

be the amplitude about zero of the steady response of [[thm-cm-forced-oscillator-sinusoidal-response]] clause 1, and put

$$u_*:=\frac{k}{m}-\frac{c^2}{2m^2},\qquad \Omega_*:=\sqrt{u_*}\ \ \text{when }u_*>0 .$$

Then:

1. If $u_*>0$ (equivalently $c^2<2mk$), $A$ is strictly increasing on $[0,\Omega_*]$, strictly decreasing on $[\Omega_*,\infty)$, and its maximum on $[0,\infty)$ is attained at $\Omega_*$ and at no other point, with
$$A(\Omega_*)=\frac{2m|f_0|}{c\sqrt{4mk-c^2}} .$$
2. If $u_*\le0$ then $A$ is strictly decreasing on $[0,\infty)$ and its maximum on $[0,\infty)$ is attained at $\Omega=0$ and at no other point.

Let $m>0$, $c\ge0$ and $k>0$, and consider the homogeneous damped oscillator model $m\,x''+c\,x'+k\,x=0$ of [[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]] with time domain $I=\mathbb R$ and forcing $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ identically zero, with characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda)=m\lambda^2+c\lambda+k$, discriminant $\Delta=c^2-4mk$, damping rate $\gamma:=c/(2m)$, and, when applicable, roots
$$\lambda_\pm:=\frac{-c\pm\sqrt\Delta}{2m}\ (\Delta\ge0),\qquad \lambda:=-\frac{c}{2m},\qquad \omega:=\frac{\sqrt{4mk-c^2}}{2m}\ (\Delta<0).$$

A local solution here may have any interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ with nonempty interior, with domain-relative derivatives at included endpoints. It has a unique extension to the global family below. A **maximal solution** means one that has no solution extension to a strictly larger interval; the maximal solutions of this global autonomous equation are precisely the family members on $\mathbb R$. For a homogeneous model restricted to a time domain $I$, its solutions have $J\subseteq I$ and are restrictions of these same global members; their extensions solve the all-$\mathbb R$ equation.

1. **Distinct real roots.** If $\Delta>0$, then $\lambda_+>\lambda_-$ are exactly the real roots of $p$, and a function $x:J\to\mathbb R$ on an interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ with nonempty interior is a solution of the model if and only if
$$x(t)=Ae^{\lambda_+t}+Be^{\lambda_-t}\quad(t\in J)$$
for some $A,B\in\mathbb R$.

2. **Double real root.** If $\Delta=0$, then $\lambda=-c/(2m)$ is the only root of $p$, and $x:J\to\mathbb R$ is a solution if and only if
$$x(t)=(A+Bt)e^{\lambda t}\quad(t\in J)$$
for some $A,B\in\mathbb R$.

3. **Complex conjugate roots.** If $\Delta<0$, then $\omega>0$, the roots of $p$ are $-\gamma\pm i\omega$, and $x:J\to\mathbb R$ is a solution if and only if
$$x(t)=e^{-\gamma t}\bigl(A\cos(\omega t)+B\sin(\omega t)\bigr)\quad(t\in J)$$
for some $A,B\in\mathbb R$.

4. **Initial data.** In each of the three cases and for every $(x_0,v_0)\in\mathbb R^2$ there is exactly one solution $x:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ with $x(0)=x_0$ and $x'(0)=v_0$. Its coefficients are
$$A=\frac{v_0-\lambda_-x_0}{\lambda_+-\lambda_-},\quad B=\frac{\lambda_+x_0-v_0}{\lambda_+-\lambda_-}\quad(\Delta>0),\qquad A=x_0,\ B=v_0-\lambda x_0\quad(\Delta=0),$$
$$A=x_0,\quad B=\frac{v_0+\gamma x_0}{\omega}\quad(\Delta<0).$$

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

1. **Velocity and acceleration** are the maps $w_i=x_i':I\to\mathbb R^3$ and $a_i=x_i'':I\to\mathbb R^3$, of dimensions $\ell\tau^{-1}$ and $\ell\tau^{-2}$ componentwise.
2. The **mass operator** is the linear map $\mathsf M:(\mathbb R^3)^N\to(\mathbb R^3)^N$, $\mathsf M(z_1,\ldots,z_N)=(m_1z_1,\ldots,m_Nz_N)$, with dimension $\mu$; the **momentum** of label $i$ is $p_i=m_iw_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$, with component dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$.
3. A **force input** is a specified map $F:I\times O\times\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N}$, where $O\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ is open, its arguments are time, positions and velocities, and each output component has dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$. No regularity or equation equating $F$ with $\mathsf M x''$ is adopted here. A later model must state both if needed.
4. For a specified scalar **potential energy** map $U:I\times O\to\mathbb R$ of dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-2}$ and a tuple $x(t)\in O$, the **kinetic energy** is $T(t)=\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^N m_i\sum_{j=1}^3(w_i(t))_j^2$, and the **mechanical energy** is $E(t)=T(t)+U(t,x(t))$. Both are real-valued and have dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-2}$; no conservation or applicability to every interaction is asserted.
5. Given a scalar map $L:I\times O\times\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R$ of the energy dimension and $t_0<t_1$ in $I$, assume $t\mapsto L(t,x(t),w(t))$ is integrable on $[t_0,t_1]$. Its **action on this curve segment** is the real number $S[x;t_0,t_1]=\int_{t_0}^{t_1}L(t,x(t),w(t))\,dt$, with dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-1}$ (the integration convention multiplies the integrand's dimension by duration). No variational principle is imposed.
6. Relative to the chosen spatial origin, define the **angular momentum** $J_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ by $J_i(t)=x_i(t)\times p_i(t)$, where for $r,s\in\mathbb R^3$ the operation is explicitly $r\times s=(r_2s_3-r_3s_2,r_3s_1-r_1s_3,r_1s_2-r_2s_1)$. Its components have dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-1}$. These quantities depend on the chosen coordinates; dimensions alone assert no transformation or conservation law.
7. A **rotation matrix** here means a real $3\times3$ matrix $R$ satisfying $R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3$ and $\det R=1$; its entries are dimensionless. A radian angle is an arc length divided by its positive radius, hence dimensionless. A generalized coordinate means a component of a specified local coordinate chart on a configuration space; each such component has its own declared dimension, and only quantities of equal dimension are added.

**(e) Conventions only.** No numerical value of any constant or parameter of a model is fixed by this item: in particular no mass, length or duration of any concrete system is asserted, and no measured value is recorded. Two numerical values that are equal but carry different dimensions are not thereby the same quantity. Where a treatment or a later item suppresses a dimensionful constant by a natural-unit convention, that convention is read as shorthand for the corresponding SI-dimensioned statement with the constant restored, and it changes no dimension fixed here.

derivations.claim: Parameters: $\omega_{0}=1$, $c\Omega=1/5$, $k-m\Omega^{2}=0$, so $D=i/5\neq0$, $\lvert D\rvert=1/5$ and $A(1)=\lvert f_{0}\rvert/\lvert D\rvert=5$ m. The general real form gives $x_{p}(t)=\cos t\cdot0+\sin t\cdot(1\cdot(1/5))/(1/25)=5\sin t$, and the substitution check is direct: $x_{p}''+cx_{p}'+kx_{p}=-5\sin t+\cos t+5\sin t=\cos t$ by [L2], so $x_{p}$ is a motion on $\mathbb R$. Taking $\delta=\pi/2$ gives $x_{p}(t)=5\cos(t-\pi/2)$ with $\cos\delta=0$ and $\sin\delta=1$: the phase lag is $\pi/2$.

Amplitude maximum: $A(\Omega)=1/\sqrt{(1-\Omega^{2})^{2}+\Omega^{2}/25}$, so its continuous extension has $A(0)=1$ and $A(1)=5$. By [L1] and $c^{2}=1/25<2mk=2$, the maximum occurs at $\Omega_{*}=\sqrt{k/m-c^{2}/(2m^{2})}=\sqrt{1-1/50}=\sqrt{49/50}$ and equals $2m\lvert f_{0}\rvert/(c\sqrt{4mk-c^{2}})=10/\sqrt{99/25}=50/(3\sqrt{11})>5$, since $3\sqrt{11}<10$ because $99<100$; hence the drive at the natural frequency is below the peak of the amplitude curve.

Transient from rest. By [L1] every motion equals $x_{p}+y$ with $y$ homogeneous; with numerical rates $\gamma=c/(2m)=1/10$ and $\omega_{d}=\sqrt{k/m-\gamma^{2}}=\sqrt{99}/10$, the homogeneous motions in numerical time are $y=e^{-t/10}(A\cos(\omega_{d}t)+B\sin(\omega_{d}t))$. The datum $(0,0,0)$ forces $A=0$ and $5+\omega_{d}B=0$ by [L2], that is $x(t)=5\sin t-(5/\omega_{d})e^{-t/10}\sin(\omega_{d}t)$, the displayed motion; it is the unique maximal motion with that datum by clause 2 of [[pthm-cm04-resonance-and-boundedness]].

Boundedness and convergence: for $t\ge0$, $\lvert x(t)\rvert\le5+(5/\omega_{d}) e^{-t/10}\le5+50/\sqrt{99}<11$, since $\sqrt{99}>9$ by [L2], and $x(t)-x_{p}(t)=-(5/\omega_{d})e^{-t/10}\sin(\omega_{d}t)\to0$ as $t\to+\infty$; differentiating the transient term with [L2] shows that it and its derivative both vanish at infinity, so $x'(t)-x_{p}'(t)\to0$; this is the convergence clause 3 of [[pthm-cm04-resonance-and-boundedness]], with the explicit decay rate $1/10$.

Undamped comparison. With $c=0$ the drive at $\Omega=\omega_{0}=1$ is the exceptional case, and clause 5 of [[pthm-cm04-resonance-and-boundedness]] gives the unbounded motion $t\sin t/2$; with $\Omega=2$ one has $D=1-4=-3$ and the steady amplitude $A(2)=1/\lvert D\rvert=1/3$ m, with every motion bounded by clause 4 of the same theorem.
