citations.quote:
Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $M:\Omega\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ be of class $C^2$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) with $M(q)$ symmetric and positive definite for every $q\in\Omega$, that is $v^{\mathsf T}M(q)v>0$ for every nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $U:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$. The matrix field $M$ is the **kinetic metric field** and $U$ the **potential** of the data in the chart $\Omega$.

Coordinates and matrix entries are indexed by $0\le i,j,k<n$, as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. Vectors are read as columns: for $A\in M_n(\mathbb R)$, $(Av)_i:=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}A_{ij}v_j$, and $v^{\mathsf T}Av:=\sum_{i,j=0}^{n-1}v_iA_{ij}v_j$.

Define, for $(q,v)\in\Omega\times\mathbb R^n$, the **kinetic energy**, **Lagrangian** and **energy**

$$T(q,v):=\tfrac12v^{\mathsf T}M(q)v,\qquad L(q,v):=T(q,v)-U(q),\qquad E(q,v):=T(q,v)+U(q),$$

and, for $q\in\Omega$ and $v\in\mathbb R^n$, the matrix

$$D_qM(q)[v]:=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}v_k\,\partial_kM(q),\qquad\bigl(\partial_kM(q)\bigr)_{ij}=\partial_kM_{ij}(q)\quad(0\le i,j,k<n).$$

The **mechanical vector field** of the data is the map

$$G:\Omega\times\mathbb R^n\longrightarrow\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n,\qquad G(q,v)=\Bigl(v,\ M(q)^{-1}\bigl(\tfrac12\nabla_q(v^{\mathsf T}M(q)v)-\bigl(D_qM(q)[v]\bigr)v-\nabla U(q)\bigr)\Bigr),$$

where $\nabla_q$ and $\nabla U$ are Euclidean gradients ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]) and $M(q)^{-1}$ is the inverse of the positive definite matrix $M(q)$ ([[def-invertible-matrix-and-general-linear-group]], [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). The **mechanical system** in the chart is the first-order system

$$q'(t)=v(t),\qquad v'(t)=M(q(t))^{-1}\Bigl(\tfrac12\nabla_qf\bigl(q(t),v(t)\bigr)-\bigl(D_qM(q(t))[v(t)]\bigr)v(t)-\nabla U(q(t))\Bigr),\qquad f(q,v):=v^{\mathsf T}M(q)v .$$

A point $q_* \in\Omega$ is a **mechanical equilibrium** when $\nabla U(q_*)=0$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $M:\Omega\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ be a $C^2$ field of symmetric positive definite matrices, let $U:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$, and let $E(q,v)=\tfrac12v^{\mathsf T}M(q)v+U(q)$ be the energy of [[def-cm-mechanical-vector-field-and-energy-in-a-chart]]. If $q:I\to\Omega$ is a $C^2$ solution of the mechanical system $M(q)q''=\tfrac12\nabla_q(q'^{\mathsf T}M(q)q')-(D_qM(q)[q'])q'-\nabla U(q)$ on the interval $I$, then

$$\frac{d}{dt}E\bigl(q(t),q'(t)\bigr)=0\qquad(t\in I);$$

that is, the energy is constant along every solution.

Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $M:\Omega\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ be a $C^2$ field of symmetric positive definite matrices, let $U:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$, let $q_0\in\Omega$ with $\nabla U(q_0)=0$, and suppose $q_0$ is a **strict local minimum** of $U$: there is $r_0>0$ with $\overline B(q_0,r_0)\subseteq\Omega$ and

$$U(q)>U(q_0)\qquad(0<\|q-q_0\|_2<r_0).$$

Let $G$ be the mechanical vector field of [[def-cm-mechanical-vector-field-and-energy-in-a-chart]] on $\Omega\times\mathbb R^n$, with energy $E(q,v)=\tfrac12v^{\mathsf T}M(q)v+U(q)$. Then $(q_0,0)$ is a Lyapunov stable equilibrium of $(q',v')=G(q,v)$ in the sense of [[def-cm-equilibrium-and-lyapunov-stability]]: for every $\varepsilon>0$ with $\overline B((q_0,0),\varepsilon)\subseteq\Omega\times\mathbb R^n$ there is $\delta>0$ such that every maximal solution $(q,v)$ with $\|(q(0),v(0))-(q_0,0)\|_2<\delta$ is defined for all $t\ge0$ and satisfies

$$\|(q(t),v(t))-(q_0,0)\|_2<\varepsilon\qquad(t\ge0).$$

No asymptotic stability is asserted.

Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $M:\Omega\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ be a $C^2$ field of symmetric positive definite matrices, let $U:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$, and let $q_0\in\Omega$ be a mechanical equilibrium, that is $\nabla U(q_0)=0$ ([[def-cm-mechanical-vector-field-and-energy-in-a-chart]]). Let $G$ be the mechanical vector field on $\Omega\times\mathbb R^n$. Then:

1. $G$ is totally differentiable at $(q_0,0)$ ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]]) and, writing $D^2U(q_0)$ for the Hessian matrix ([[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]]),

$$DG(q_0,0)(\delta q,\delta v)=\Bigl(\delta v,\ -M(q_0)^{-1}D^2U(q_0)\,\delta q\Bigr)\qquad(\delta q,\delta v\in\mathbb R^n);$$

2. consequently the linearised equation at the equilibrium is

$$\xi''=-M(q_0)^{-1}D^2U(q_0)\,\xi,\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad M(q_0)\xi''+D^2U(q_0)\,\xi=0,$$

a constant-coefficient system whose mass matrix $M(q_0)$ is symmetric positive definite and whose stiffness matrix $D^2U(q_0)$ is symmetric ([[cor-hessian-is-symmetric]]);
3. if in addition $q_0$ is a strict local minimum of $U$, then $K:=D^2U(q_0)$ is non-negative, so the hypotheses of [[thm-cm-quadratic-mode-decomposition]] are satisfied by $M(q_0)$ and $K$, and the linearised system is exactly the constant-coefficient quadratic system of that theorem with mass matrix $M(q_0)$ and stiffness $K$; its modes are the normal modes of the linearisation.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]). If $f$ is differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) then $f$ is continuous at $c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

Consequently, if $f$ is differentiable on a set $S \subseteq A$ then $f$ is
continuous at every point of $S$.

**No converse is asserted, and none holds.** Continuity at $c$ does not give
differentiability at $c$, and the standard witness is worked out on the
companion page.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=m\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z,\qquad \cos x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=(m+1/2)\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z.$$
Both sine and cosine have period $2\pi$, and no smaller positive number is a common period.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Let $g>0$ and $l>0$, put $\omega:=(g/l)^{1/2}>0$ ([[thm-of-square-roots]]), and define the field

$$F:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2,\qquad F(\theta,v):=\bigl(v,-\omega^2\sin\theta\bigr),$$

so that $z'=F(z)$ for $z=(\theta,v)$ is the first-order form of the pendulum equation
$\theta''=-\omega^2\sin\theta$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]] for the
componentwise first-order reduction). Put

$$A:=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-\omega^2&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad L:=\max\{1,\omega^2\}.$$

Then:

1. $F$ is of class $C^\infty$ (in particular continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state
   variable), $F(0)=0$, $A=DF(0)$ is the total derivative of $F$ at the origin, and for every
   $r>0$ and every $z=(\theta,v)$ with $\lVert z\rVert_2\le r$ ([[def-metric-ball]] for the ball,
   [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] for the norm)

$$\lVert F(z)-Az\rVert_2=\omega^2\lvert\sin\theta-\theta\rvert\le\frac{\omega^2}{6}\lvert\theta\rvert^3\le\frac{\omega^2r}{6}\lVert z\rVert_2^2,\qquad\lVert F(z)\rVert_2\le L\lVert z\rVert_2 ;$$

   moreover $F$ is globally Lipschitz in the state variable with constant $L$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]), and the operator norm of $A$ for the Euclidean norm is
   $\lVert A\rVert=L$ ([[def-operator-norm]]);
2. let $z_0\in\mathbb R^2$ with $\delta:=\lVert z_0\rVert_2>0$, let $T>0$ and $r>0$ satisfy
   $\delta e^{LT}<r$, and let $y:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^2$ be the solution of the linear initial
   value problem $y'=Ay$, $y(0)=z_0$
   ([[cor-cm-variation-of-constants-for-linear-systems]]). Then the maximal solution $z$ of
   $z'=F(z)$, $z(0)=z_0$, is defined on $[0,T]$ with $\lVert z(t)\rVert_2\le\delta e^{Lt}$ for
   $t\in[0,T]$, and for every $t\in[0,T]$

$$\lVert z(t)-y(t)\rVert_2\le\frac{\omega^2r}{6}\delta^2\int_0^te^{\lVert A\rVert(t-s)}e^{2Ls}\,ds\le\frac{\omega^2r}{6}\delta^2\,t\,e^{(\lVert A\rVert+2L)t}$$

   ([[thm-cm-finite-time-linearization-error-bound]]);
3. the linear system $y'=Ay$ is the linearised pendulum: writing $y=(y_1,y_2)$ one has
   $y_1''=-\omega^2y_1$ and $y_2=y_1'$, and the first components satisfy
   $\lvert z_1(t)-y_1(t)\rvert\le\lVert z(t)-y(t)\rVert_2$ with the bounds of clause 2. The
   estimate is a finite-time statement of order $\delta^2$: it neither states nor implies that the
   nonlinear pendulum is exactly harmonic, and it makes no claim beyond $[0,T]$.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

derivations.claim: Angular potential. By [L2], $U'(\theta)=mgl\sin\theta=-F(\theta)$; the generalized torque is therefore the negative derivative of the declared energy-valued scalar potential $U(\theta)=-mgl\cos\theta$. The equilibria are the zeros of $\sin\theta$, namely $\theta=n\pi$, $n\in\mathbb Z$; and $\theta=0$ is a strict local minimum because $U(0)=-mgl$ and $U(\theta)=-mgl\cos\theta>-mgl$ for $0<|\theta|<\pi$ by [L2]. This is claim 1.

Stability. By [L1] and step 1.1 the hanging rest point $(0,0)$ is Lyapunov stable for the model's phase system, with the Euclidean phase norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and the balls of [[def-metric-ball]].

Linearisation and frequency: $U''(\theta)=mgl\cos\theta$, so $U''(0)=mgl>0$; by the linearisation clause of [L1] the linearised angular equation at $\theta=0$ is $m_{\mathrm{ef}}\xi''+mgl\xi=0$. Its angular frequency is $\omega=\sqrt{U''(0)/m_{\mathrm{ef}}}=\sqrt{mgl/(ml^{2})}=\sqrt{g/l}$ by [[thm-of-square-roots]]. In the source's reading this is the small-oscillation frequency of the ideal pendulum model. This is claim 2.

Small-angle bound at $g=l=1$. Here $\omega^{2}=1$, $L=\max\{1,1\}=1$, $\lVert DF_{p}(0)\rVert=1$, and every explicitly quantified datum $z_0$ in claim 3 has $\omega^{2}r/6=1/12$, $\delta^{2}=10^{-4}$. The hypothesis $\delta e^{LT}<r$ reads $10^{-2}e<1/2$, which holds since $e<3<50$ by [L4]. By [L3] the exact solution and the linearised solution (which solves $\theta''=-\theta$, the numerical linearized chart equation with coefficient $\omega^2=1$) obey $$\lVert z(t)-y(t)\rVert_{2}\le\frac{1}{12}\cdot\frac{1}{10^{4}}\cdot t\,e^{3t}=\frac{t\,e^{3t}}{12\cdot10^{4}}\qquad(0\le t\le1),$$ and at $t=1$ this is at most $e^{3}/(12\cdot10^{4})$, which is less than $27/(12\cdot10^{4})=\tfrac94\cdot10^{-4}$ by [L4]. This is claim 3.

The quadratic energy of the linearised angular equation is not conserved. Along a motion of the exact model, $$\frac{d}{dt}E_{\rm quad}=\frac{d}{dt}\Bigl[\tfrac12m_{\mathrm{ef}}\theta'^{2}+\tfrac12mgl\theta^{2}\Bigr]=m_{\mathrm{ef}}\theta'\theta''+mgl\,\theta\theta'=mgl\,\theta'\bigl(\theta-\sin\theta\bigr)$$ by [L2] and the equation of motion $m_{\mathrm{ef}}\theta''=-mgl\sin\theta$. At the phase point $(\theta,\theta')=(\pi/2,1\,\mathrm{s^{-1}})$ the right side equals $mgl(1\,\mathrm{s^{-1}})(\pi/2-\sin(\pi/2))>0$. Indeed $\sin(\pi/2)=1<\pi/2$: the mean value theorem applied to sine on $[0,\pi/2]$ gives $1=\cos\xi\cdot(\pi/2)$ for some $\xi\in(0,\pi/2)$, with $\cos\xi<1$. Thus the quadratic energy changes along the exact pendulum motion, so the exact angular equation is not its linearised equation. This is claim 4.

boundaries.reason: The check declares one model with fixed positive data; no possibly empty family is quantified.

boundaries.evidence: The equilibrium point theta=0 is the strict minimum of step 1.1 and the stable rest point of step 2.1; the zero-amplitude case is the rest motion and is not the declared datum of step 3.1.
The effective model is one-dimensional in the angle coordinate; the potential check of step 1.1, the frequency of step 2.2 and the error bound of step 3.1 are scalar.
The linearisation is applied at the nondegenerate strict minimum with U''(0)=mgl>0; the vanishing-curvature case is excluded by the hypothesis of the linearisation clause, as stated at step 2.2.

The small-angle error bound of step 3.1 is stated on 0<=t<=1, a compact interval with the datum at its left endpoint t=0; the mean value application for pi/2-1>0 at step 4.1 uses the interior of [0,pi/2].

boundaries.reason: The nonlinearity of the model is exhibited at a single phase point; no selection from a family is made.
The check verifies the model, its potential presentation and the error bound; it is not stated as an equivalence.

The Example verifies an effective pendulum potential, its local linearization error and a failure of harmonic-energy conservation; these comparisons do not assert a converse characterization of nonlinear pendulums.

risk_review.notes: Checked all five steps and mathematical chart/small-angle suppliers. Angular coordinate has generalized inertia ml² and torque -mgl sin theta; it is explicitly adopted rather than imported from translational postulates. U is C2, zero is strict minimum, linearized coefficient positive. Numerical SI time at g=l=1 gives L=||A||=1, delta e<r, and bound e³/120000=0.0001673795. Quadratic-energy derivative positive at (pi/2,1/s) by MVT. Likharev Eq 1.18 independently read and visually checked on PDF page 10 / printed page 6; source locator corrected. No measurement or all-time approximation asserted.

citations.quote:
**(i) Setting.** Work in the one-dimensional model class of
[[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]] with time window
$I_{0}=\mathbb R$, configuration domain $Q=\mathbb R$, mass $m>0$, spring
constant $k>0$ ([[post-cm04-harmonic-model]]) and drag coefficient $c\ge0$
([[post-cm04-linear-damping-model]]). Let a real **drive amplitude**
$f_{0}\in\mathbb R$ of dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$ (newtons) and an
**angular drive frequency** $\Omega>0$ of dimension $\tau^{-1}$ (radians per
second; the radian is dimensionless in the framework's angle convention,
[[def-cm01-units]]) be declared. Adopt, through the additive composition of
force contributions of clause (v) of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] and
the external-contribution reading of [[post-cm02-interactions]], the force
law
$$F(t,x,v):=f_{0}\cos(\Omega t)-k\,x-c\,v .$$
The **sinusoidally driven oscillator model** is the one-dimensional model
with this force law; its equation of motion is
$$m\,x''+c\,x'+k\,x=f_{0}\cos(\Omega t),$$
and its data $(m,c,k,f)$ with $f(t)=f_{0}\cos(\Omega t)$ are oscillator-type
data in the sense of clause (f) of
[[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]]. The term
$f_{0}\cos(\Omega t)$ is the **drive** or **driving force**; the model is
undamped when $c=0$ and strictly damped when $c>0$.

**(ii) The drive is prescribed external data.** The driving force is a
prescribed function of time alone: it does not depend on $x$ or on $x'$, and
the object producing it is not one of the model's labels and is not modelled
dynamically. This is the same modelling status as the medium of
[[post-cm02-drag]]: the drive is an external contribution declared as part
of the model. A real apparatus, background or force generator that reacts to
the motion is **not** represented by this model; representing such a
back-reaction requires a larger model with additional states.

**(iii) Potential presentation with residual force.** The model presents its
force law through the harmonic potential $U(x)=\tfrac12kx^{2}$ with residual
force $d(t,x,v)=f_{0}\cos(\Omega t)-c\,v$, in the sense of clause (d) of
[[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]]:
$F(t,x,v)=-U'(x)+d(t,x,v)$. The mechanical energy of the model is
$E(x,v)=\tfrac12mv^{2}+\tfrac12kx^{2}$ of that clause, defined along every
motion; the model is driven and not a global potential model whenever
$f_{0}\neq0$.

**(iv) Regularity.** Let $X:=x_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm m)$,
$V:=v_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm{m/s})$, and $T:=t_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm s)$
be the dimensionless numerical SI coordinates (the real inputs of the force
map). Write
$K:=k_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm{N/m})$,
$C:=c_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm{kg/s})$,
$\widehat f_{0}:=f_{0}/(1\,\mathrm N)$, and
$\widehat\Omega:=\Omega(1\,\mathrm s)$. The numerical force map is
$$\widehat F(T,X,V)=\widehat f_{0}\cos(\widehat\Omega T)-KX-CV,$$
so it is continuous and globally Lipschitz in the state variable with
numerical-coordinate constant $K+C$, uniformly in time. This is a bound on
dimensionless SI coordinates and force values, not a sum of the dimensionful
$k$ and $c$ ([[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]). It is an
admissible force law of clause (a) of [[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]],
and its equation is the forced model $m\,x''+cx'+kx=f$ of
[[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]] with the continuous function
$f(t)=f_{0}\cos(\Omega t)$.

**(v) Physical status and regime.** The model is a **restricted idealization**
adopted rather than derived: exactly sinusoidal, with constant amplitude and
frequency and no dependence on the motion. The drive amplitude and frequency
are model parameters; when their values come from an apparatus calibration,
that use is an empirical premise carrying the apparatus conditions and the
measurement uncertainty, and this item asserts no such value. The sinusoidal
form is the elementary component used by the recorded treatments; the
response to a non-sinusoidal periodic drive is a superposition statement
belonging to the mathematical theory, not an additional claim here. The
model's undamped case $c=0$ is included as a parameter value, and it is where
the resonant unboundedness of the following theorem occurs.

**(vi) Status.** Adopted assumption of the framework when a model invokes
it; it selects no law of nature on its own, and no measured response, no
resonance curve of any apparatus and no empirical resonance phenomenon is
asserted by the postulate.

**(a) Data of a one-dimensional model.** A **one-dimensional model** is
declared by the following data: a fixed positive **mass** $m>0$, of dimension
$\mu$ read in kilograms ([[def-cm01-units]], [[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause
(v)); a **time window** $I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$, a nondegenerate open
interval read in seconds ([[def-interval]]); an open **configuration
domain** $Q\subseteq\mathbb R$, a nonempty open interval of the real line
read in metres; and a **force law**
$$F:I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad (t,x,v)\longmapsto F(t,x,v),$$
of dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$, read in newtons, subject to the **standing
regularity** of the framework: $F$ is continuous on $I_{0}\times Q\times
\mathbb R$ and locally Lipschitz in the state variable $(x,v)$ locally
uniformly in time ([[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]). The
framework's three-dimensional force branch is
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]]; the class declared here is a **restricted
model class** adopted at the same primitive level, in which the physical
position of a single label along one coordinate is the whole state. A model
whose force law fails the standing regularity is not a one-dimensional model
of this class. When a statement differentiates the force law or the potential,
the additional smoothness it needs is stated in that statement.

**(b) Motions.** Let $J\subseteq I_{0}$ be an interval with nonempty interior
(endpoints read with one-sided derivatives, as in
[[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]). A **motion** of
the model on $J$ is a curve $x:J\to Q$ of class $C^{2}$
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]) with
$$m\,x''(t)=F\bigl(t,x(t),x'(t)\bigr)\qquad(t\in J).$$
In the notation of the three-dimensional branch this is the scalar
restriction of its equation of motion clause (iv) to a single coordinate; the
motions of the present class are declared to be these curves. A **datum** at
time $t_{0}\in I_{0}$ is a triple $(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})$ with $x_{0}\in Q$ and
$v_{0}\in\mathbb R$; a motion $x$ **takes** the datum when $x(t_{0})=x_{0}$
and $x'(t_{0})=v_{0}$.

**(c) Phase system.** The **phase system** of the model is the first-order
system on the open set $I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R\subseteq\mathbb R^{3}$
with right-hand side
$$G_{F}(t,x,v):=\Bigl(v,\ \frac{F(t,x,v)}{m}\Bigr),$$
read as a system of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]];
its state variable is $z=(x,v)$. For an interval $J\subseteq I_0$ with
nonempty interior, a **phase solution** on $J$ means a differentiable curve
$z:J\to Q\times\mathbb R$ satisfying $z'(t)=G_F(t,z(t))$ for every $t\in J$,
with domain-relative derivatives at included endpoints. Equivalently, for
any $t_0\in J$ it is a solution in the cited IVP sense with datum
$(t_0,z(t_0))$. For a $C^2$ curve $x:J\to Q$, being a motion is equivalent
to $t\mapsto(x(t),x'(t))$ being a phase solution: the first component is
$x'=v$ and the second is $x''=F(t,x,x')/m$. Conversely a phase solution
$(x,v)$ has $x'=v$ and $v'=F(t,x,v)/m$; continuity of $F$ makes $v'$ continuous,
so $x$ is $C^2$ and is a motion. This is the argument of clause (c) of
[[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]] read in one
coordinate. Here $x$ is the **position** or **displacement** coordinate and
$v$ the **velocity** coordinate; both are read in the fixed inertial frame in
which the model is declared. The phase system inherits the standing
regularity: $G_{F}$ is continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable
locally uniformly in time, so the Picard–Lindelöf hypotheses of
[[thm-picard-lindelof-local-existence-and-uniqueness]] hold at every point of
its domain.

**(d) Potential presentation, residual forces and energy.** The model
**presents its force law through a potential** when it declares a function
$U:Q\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^{2}$ in the sense of clause (a) of
[[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]] of dimension
$\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$, read in joules, and a **residual force**
$d:I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ of the standing regularity of
(a), with
$$F(t,x,v)=-U'(x)+d(t,x,v)\qquad\bigl((t,x,v)\in I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R\bigr);$$
here $U'$ is the ordinary derivative. This is the one-coordinate case of the
potential presentation of [[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]] clause
(a) for a time- and velocity-independent potential, and the scalar
$U$ is a **potential energy** of the model's potential part. The model is a
**global potential model** (equivalently, in the framework's usage, a
**conservative model**) when $d\equiv0$; the term "conservative" is used only
in this sense, as recorded in that definition. For a conservative model the
**mechanical energy** is the function
$$E:Q\times\mathbb R\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad E(x,v):=\tfrac12 m v^{2}+U(x),$$
of dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$. For a model with declared residual
forces, the **mechanical energy along a motion** $x:J\to Q$ is
$E(t):=\tfrac12m\,x'(t)^{2}+U(x(t))$; it is defined along curve families even
though the force law is not presented through $U$ alone.

**(e) Equilibria.** A **time- and velocity-independent force law** on $Q$ is
one of the form $F(t,x,v)=f(x)$ for a function $f:Q\to\mathbb R$; the model
is then **autonomous**. For such a law, a point $x_{*}\in Q$ is an
**equilibrium** (or **rest position**) when $f(x_{*})=0$, and the phase-plane
point $(x_{*},0)$ is the corresponding **rest point** of the phase system;
the constant curve $x\equiv x_{*}$ is then a motion. When the force law is
presented as $f=-U'$ with $U$ of class $C^{2}$, the equilibria are exactly
the critical points of $U$:
$f(x_{*})=0\iff U'(x_{*})=0$. A point $x_{0}\in Q$ is a **strict local
minimum** of $U$ when $U(x)>U(x_{0})$ for every $x\in Q$ with $0<\lvert
x-x_{0}\rvert<r_{0}$ for some $r_{0}>0$. The **Lyapunov stability** and
**asymptotic stability** of a rest point of the autonomous phase system are
the notions of [[def-cm-equilibrium-and-lyapunov-stability]] applied to the
field $G_{F}$; they are not defined here anew.

**(f) Oscillator-type data.** Let $m>0$, $c\ge0$, $k\in\mathbb R$ and let
$f:I_{0}\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. A model **is of oscillator type with
data $(m,c,k,f)$** when its force law has the form
$$F(t,x,v)=f(t)-c\,v-k\,x\qquad\bigl((t,x,v)\in I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R\bigr)$$
with $Q$ a nonempty open interval containing $0$ when the equation is read
about the origin, and the parameters are read with dimensions $[c]=\mu\tau^{-1}$
(kilograms per second), $[k]=\mu\tau^{-2}$ (kilograms per second squared) and
$[f]=\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$ (newtons). For such a model the equation of motion is
the second-order equation $m\,x''+c\,x'+k\,x=f(t)$, and the motions are
exactly the restrictions of the solutions of the mathematical model of
[[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]] with the same data, by the
identification of that definition's phase system with the phase system (c).
The parameters $c$ and $k$ are model data: they enter the model's declaration
and are not derived by this item.

**(g) Status.** This item introduces vocabulary, objects, regularity and
dimensions; it contains no existence, uniqueness, conservation, stability or
boundedness assertion, no force law of nature and no measured value. In
particular, clause (a) **declares** the one-dimensional class rather than
deriving it from the three-dimensional branch, and clauses (d)-(f) only fix
which data a model of the class carries. Every later statement of this page
names the model data, the potential representative and the initial datum it
uses.

Let $m>0$, $c\ge0$ and $k\in\mathbb R$ be given real numbers, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $f:I\to\mathbb R$ be continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). The **damped driven oscillator model** with data $(m,c,k,f)$ is the second-order equation

$$m\,x''(t)+c\,x'(t)+k\,x(t)=f(t),\qquad t\in I .$$

A **solution** of the model on an interval $J\subseteq I$ with nonempty interior is a twice differentiable $x:J\to\mathbb R$ such that the identity holds for every $t\in J$, derivatives being ordinary real derivatives ([[def-derivative]], [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). The model is called **homogeneous** when $f\equiv 0$, **undamped** when $c=0$, and **strictly damped** when $c>0$.

The **phase-plane equation** of the model has right-hand side

$$G_f:I\times\mathbb R^2\longrightarrow\mathbb R^2,\qquad G_f(t,x,v):=\Bigl(v,\ \frac{f(t)-c\,v-k\,x}{m}\Bigr).$$

Here $\mathbb R^2$ is the **phase plane**, with coordinates $(x,v)$, where $x$ is the **displacement** and $v$ the **velocity**. For an interval $J\subseteq I$ with nonempty interior, a differentiable curve $z=(x,v):J\to\mathbb R^2$ solves the phase-plane equation when $z'(t)=G_f(t,z(t))$ for every $t\in J$, using the domain-relative derivative at any included endpoint ([[def-derivative]]). If $x$ is a solution of the model on $J$, then $t\mapsto(x(t),x'(t))$ solves this equation; conversely, if $t\mapsto(x(t),v(t))$ solves it, then $v=x'$ and $x$ is a solution of the model on $J$. When $J$ is open, this is the first-order system of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]] on the open domain $J\times\mathbb R^2$. For the homogeneous model the right-hand side is written $G_0(x,v)=(v,-(cv+kx)/m)$.

The **characteristic polynomial** of the model is

$$p(\lambda):=m\lambda^2+c\lambda+k,$$

with **discriminant** $\Delta:=c^2-4mk$. When $k>0$ define the **undamped frequency** $\omega_0:=\sqrt{k/m}$, the **damping rate** $\gamma:=c/(2m)$ and, when $4mk>c^2$, the **damped frequency** $\omega:=\sqrt{k/m-\gamma^2}=\sqrt{4mk-c^2}/(2m)$; the corresponding square roots are the nonnegative real ones.

Adopt the sinusoidally driven oscillator model of
[[post-cm04-sinusoidal-drive-model]] with data $m>0$, $k>0$, $c\ge0$,
$f_{0}\in\mathbb R$ and $\Omega>0$, force law
$F(t,x,v)=f_{0}\cos(\Omega t)-kx-cv$ and equation
$m\,x''+cx'+kx=f_{0}\cos(\Omega t)$. Put
$$\omega_{0}:=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}},\qquad D:=k-m\Omega^{2}+i\,c\,\Omega\in\mathbb C,$$
and define the **steady response**
$$x_{p}(t):=\operatorname{Re}\Bigl(\frac{f_{0}e^{i\Omega t}}{D}\Bigr) =\frac{f_{0}\bigl[(k-m\Omega^{2})\cos(\Omega t)+c\,\Omega\sin(\Omega t)\bigr]} {(k-m\Omega^{2})^{2}+c^{2}\Omega^{2}}\qquad(D\neq0),$$
with **amplitude** $A(\Omega):=\lvert f_{0}\rvert/\sqrt{(k-m\Omega^{2})^{2}+c^{2}\Omega^{2}}$,
and in the exceptional case $c=0$, $\Omega=\omega_{0}$ define
$x_{p}(t):=f_{0}t\sin(\omega_{0}t)/(2m\omega_{0})$. All all-time boundedness, convergence and unboundedness claims below refer to maximal motions on $\mathbb R$; local motions are their restrictions as in clause 2. Then:

1. **Steady response.** If $D\neq0$ — that is $c>0$, or $c=0$ and
   $\Omega\neq\omega_{0}$ — then $x_{p}$ is a motion of the model on
   $\mathbb R$, of period $2\pi/\Omega$, with amplitude $A(\Omega)$ in the
   sense $\lvert x_{p}(t)\rvert\le A(\Omega)$ for all $t$ and equality at
   suitable times.
2. **Reduction to the homogeneous model.** Every datum has exactly one
   maximal motion, it is defined on all of $\mathbb R$, and every motion
   $x$ of the model on an interval with nonempty interior can be written
   $x=x_{p}+y$, where $x_{p}$ is the particular motion of clause 1, or the
   resonant motion in the exceptional case, and $y$ is a motion of the damped
   homogeneous model with the same $m$, $c$, $k$ (and is a harmonic motion
   of [[post-cm04-harmonic-model]] when $c=0$).
3. **Strictly damped case $c>0$.** For every $\Omega>0$ the following hold:
  every motion is bounded on $[0,\infty)$; and
   $x(t)-x_{p}(t)\to0$ and $x'(t)-x_{p}'(t)\to0$ as $t\to+\infty$. Moreover
   $x_{p}$ is the unique motion with datum
   $(t_{0},x_{p}(t_{0}),x_{p}'(t_{0}))$ for any $t_{0}\in\mathbb R$. The
   amplitude function $\Omega\mapsto A(\Omega)$ has the following shape when $f_0\ne0$: if
   $c^{2}<2mk$ it is strictly increasing on $(0,\Omega_{*})$ and strictly
   decreasing on $(\Omega_{*},\infty)$, so has its unique maximum there, with
   $$\Omega_{*}=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}-\frac{c^{2}}{2m^{2}}},\qquad A(\Omega_{*})=\frac{2m\lvert f_{0}\rvert}{c\sqrt{4mk-c^{2}}};$$
   if $c^{2}\ge2mk$ it is strictly decreasing on $(0,\infty)$ and does not
   attain a maximum on the declared positive-frequency domain. Its continuous
   extension to $\Omega=0$ has its maximum there. For $f_0=0$ the amplitude is
   identically zero on the domain, so every frequency has the same value.
4. **Undamped case away from resonance.** For $c=0$ and
   $\Omega\neq\omega_{0}$ every motion is bounded on $\mathbb R$.
5. **Undamped resonance.** For $c=0$, $\Omega=\omega_{0}$ and $f_{0}\neq0$
   the motion $x_{p}(t)=f_{0}t\sin(\omega_{0}t)/(2m\omega_{0})$ is unbounded
   on $[0,\infty)$, and every motion of the model is unbounded on
   $[0,\infty)$, although the drive $t\mapsto f_{0}\cos(\omega_{0}t)$ is
   bounded.
6. **Off the singular cases.** For $c>0$ the denominator never vanishes and
   every $\Omega>0$ is admissible; for $c=0$ the exceptional frequency is
   exactly $\Omega=\omega_{0}$. Consequently the boundedness assertions of
   clauses 3 and 4 hold for $c>0$, and for $c=0$ away from $\Omega=\omega_{0}$,
   and also at undamped resonance when $f_0=0$; for a nonzero drive clause 5 gives unboundedness at undamped resonance.

Let $m>0$, $k>0$, $c\ge0$, let $f_0\in\mathbb R$ and $\Omega\ge0$, and consider the forced model $m\,x''+c\,x'+k\,x=f$ with time domain $I=\mathbb R$ and forcing $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, $f(t)=f_0\cos(\Omega t)$ ([[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]]). Put

$$D:=k-m\Omega^2+i\,c\,\Omega\in\mathbb C,\qquad \omega_0:=\sqrt{k/m}.$$

1. **Non-resonant response.** If $D\ne0$, then the function
$$x_p(t):=\operatorname{Re}\!\left(\frac{f_0e^{i\Omega t}}{D}\right)=f_0\,\frac{(k-m\Omega^2)\cos(\Omega t)+c\,\Omega\sin(\Omega t)}{(k-m\Omega^2)^2+c^2\Omega^2}$$
is a solution of the forced model on all of $\mathbb R$. Its amplitude about zero is $|f_0|/\sqrt{(k-m\Omega^2)^2+c^2\Omega^2}$. For $\Omega>0$ and $f_0\ne0$, a **phase-lag angle relative to the drive** means a real $\phi$ such that $x_p(t)=(f_0/|D|)\cos(\Omega t-\phi)$ for every $t$, with the signed factor $f_0$ retained in both drive and response. Such an angle exists: any $\phi\in\mathbb R$ satisfying
$$\cos\phi=\frac{k-m\Omega^2}{|D|},\qquad\sin\phi=\frac{c\Omega}{|D|}$$
has this property. No temporal phase is assigned when $\Omega=0$ or $f_0=0$.

2. **Resonance.** If $c=0$ and $\Omega=\omega_0$, then $D=0$ and
$$x_p(t):=\frac{f_0\,t\sin(\omega_0t)}{2m\omega_0}$$
is a solution of the forced model on all of $\mathbb R$; if $f_0\ne0$ then $x_p$ is unbounded on $[0,\infty)$.

3. **Transient decay.** If $c>0$, then $D\ne0$ for every $\Omega\ge0$, and every solution $x:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ of the forced model satisfies
$$x(t)=x_p(t)+x_h(t)$$
where $x_h$ is a homogeneous solution; consequently $x(t)-x_p(t)\to0$ as $t\to+\infty$ ([[def-limits-at-infinity]]) and $x$ is bounded on $[0,\infty)$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

Throughout, $+\infty$ and $-\infty$ are **abbreviations and not real numbers**,
exactly as in [[def-interval]] and [[def-divergence-to-infinity]]. Every phrase
below is a single abbreviation for a displayed condition on reals, and no
arithmetic is ever performed with the symbols.

**Limits at $+\infty$.** Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be **not bounded above**
([[def-bounded-set]]), let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$. We
write

$$\lim_{x \to +\infty} f(x) = L$$

when for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real $M$ such that

$$|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon \qquad \text{for every } x \in A \text{ with } x > M .$$

**Limits at $-\infty$.** Let $A$ be **not bounded below**. We write
$\lim_{x \to -\infty} f(x) = L$ when for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a
real $M$ with $|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon$ for every $x \in A$ with $x < M$.

**Why unboundedness is required.** It plays exactly the role the limit-point
condition plays in [[def-function-limit]]. Saying that $A$ is not bounded above
says that no real is an upper bound of $A$, that is, that for every real $M$
there is $x \in A$ with $x > M$ ([[def-bounded-set]],
[[def-complete-ordered-field]]); so the set over which the condition quantifies
is never empty and the condition is never vacuous. Without the hypothesis every
real $L$ would satisfy it and the notation would not denote.

**Uniqueness, proved here.** Suppose $A$ is not bounded above and
$\lim_{x \to +\infty} f(x) = L$ and $\lim_{x \to +\infty} f(x) = L'$ with
$L \ne L'$. Then $|L - L'| > 0$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]]), so
$\varepsilon := |L - L'|/2 > 0$ ([[cor-of-one-positive]],
[[lem-of-inverse-positive]], [[lem-of-sign-rules]]). Choose reals $M_1, M_2$
witnessing the two conditions at this $\varepsilon$ and let $M$ be the larger of
them, the order being total. Since $A$ is not bounded above there is $x \in A$
with $x > M$, hence with $x > M_1$ and $x > M_2$, and then

$$|L - L'| = |(L - f(x)) + (f(x) - L')| \le |f(x) - L| + |f(x) - L'| < 2\varepsilon = |L - L'|$$

([[lem-of-triangle-inequality]], [[lem-of-abs-value]], [[lem-of-add-order]]),
which trichotomy forbids. So $L = L'$, and the notation
$\lim_{x \to +\infty} f(x)$ denotes a single real. The same four lines, with the
inequalities on $x$ reversed, give uniqueness at $-\infty$.

**Infinite limits at a point.** Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c$ be a limit
point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) and let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$. We write

$$f(x) \to +\infty \ \text{ as } \ x \to c$$

when for every real $M$ there is a real $\delta > 0$ such that $f(x) > M$ for
every $x \in A$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$; and $f(x) \to -\infty$ as $x \to c$
when for every real $M$ there is a real $\delta > 0$ with $f(x) < M$ for every
such $x$.

**This library does not write $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = +\infty$.** The right-hand
side would not be an element of $\mathbb{R}$, and writing the equation would
silently move the discussion into the extended real line, a structure that is
not a field. That is the convention already fixed by
[[def-divergence-to-infinity]] for sequences and by [[rem-sup-conventions]] for
suprema, and it is kept here. In particular none of the rules of
[[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]] may be applied to a function tending to
$\pm\infty$.

**Combined forms.** Let $A$ be not bounded above and $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$. We
write $f(x) \to +\infty$ as $x \to +\infty$ when for every real $N$ there is a
real $M$ with $f(x) > N$ for every $x \in A$ with $x > M$. The other forms are
obtained the same way, by pairing one of the two conditions on $x$ (unbounded
above, unbounded below) with one of the two conditions on $f(x)$ (above every
real, below every real); each is again a single abbreviation for the displayed
condition, and none of them is an equation.

derivations.claim: Take the model data $m=1\ \mathrm{kg}$, $k=1\ \mathrm{N/m}$, $c=0$, $f_{0}=1\ \mathrm{N}$, $\Omega=1\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$, so that $\omega_{0}=1$ and the drive is $t\mapsto\cos t$; it is bounded: $\lvert\cos t\rvert\le1$ for all $t$ by [L4]. The hypothesis of the refuted statement therefore holds for this model.

By [L2] the function $x_{p}(t)=t\sin t/2$ is a motion of this model on $\mathbb R$. At the times $t_{k}=\pi/2+2\pi k$, $k\in\mathbb N$, one has $\sin t_{k}=1$ and hence $x_{p}(t_{k})=t_{k}/2\to+\infty$ as $k\to\infty$ by [L4]; therefore $x_{p}$ is not bounded on $[0,\infty)$, and the conclusion of the refuted statement fails.

In fact every maximal motion of this model is unbounded on $[0,\infty)$: by [L2] it equals $x_{p}+y$ on $\mathbb R$ with $y$ harmonic, and a bounded $y$ cannot compensate the unbounded $x_{p}$. Local motions are restrictions of these maximal motions; no unboundedness is claimed for a restriction to a bounded time interval. Hence the refuted statement fails at the level of a declared model of the framework, not merely through one exceptional solution.

The failure exhibited here is specific to the nonzero resonant drive. For the same $m,k,f_{0},\Omega$ but with $c=1/5>0$, [L3] gives that every maximal motion is bounded; and for $c=0$ but with $\Omega=2\neq\omega_{0}$, [L3] again gives that every maximal motion is bounded. Clause 6 also records the zero-drive resonant case: when $c=0$, $\Omega=\omega_{0}$ and $f_{0}=0$, the equation is homogeneous and every maximal motion is bounded. Thus this example refutes the implication for nonzero undamped resonant data, while the stated bounded cases remain bounded.
